path.subtitle: Cut the boring 80%; protect the human 20%
path.summary: Teaching has two parts. The boring 80%, which is photocopying worksheets, drafting feedback stems, formatting question papers, summarising NCERT chapters; and the human 20%, which is reading a child's face and deciding when to push, when to wait. AI does the first part well and the second part terribly. This path makes that line crisp, hands you a working playbook for prep, assessment and classroom honesty, and ends with a 14-day experiment you actually run with your own students.

blocks.md:
Teaching is two jobs that share a body. The first job is the boring 80%: photocopying, drafting feedback stems, summarising chapters, formatting question papers, writing the same parent email for the fifteenth time. The second job is the human 20%: looking at a tired Class 10 student before a board exam and deciding to spend a minute, not a lecture.

AI is excellent at the first job. AI is *terrible* at the second job. Most of the trouble in this entire field comes from people not drawing the line. By the end of this lesson, the line will feel obvious. The rest of the course is just learning to walk it.

blocks.title: Mental model: AI is a fluent intern who has never met your students
blocks.md:
Picture a smart, fast, exhausting intern. Speaks in full paragraphs. Knows the textbook. Has never sat in your second-period Class 8 and watched Aarav fall asleep three times because his father lost his job last week.

The intern is *useful* for everything that doesn't require having met Aarav. The intern is *dangerous* the moment you ask it to make a call that depends on having met Aarav. The whole skill of using AI in teaching is knowing which side of that line you're on.

blocks.caption: Drag tasks across the line. Watch the AI intern handle the left side and freeze on the right.

hi-IN.title: Apna analogy — *student teacher* wala
hi-IN.md:
Bhai, scene yeh hai. Naya student teacher aaya hai school mein. B.Ed final year. English hi-fi. Bachchon ke naam ek nahi yaad.

Worksheet bana de? Bilkul, kar dega — neat, time pe.

Aarav ke papa ki naukri chali gayi, uss baccha se baat kar — *yeh* tu khud kar. Student teacher ko mat bhej. Wahi galti AI ke saath bhi mat kar.

en.title: Same point, no Hinglish
en.md: A new student teacher arrives. Polished, eager, knows the syllabus, doesn't yet know which child has which weight on his shoulders. You'd let them draft a worksheet; you wouldn't send them to handle a parent grief call. Treat AI exactly the same way.

blocks.md:
Before you open Claude or ChatGPT, ask one question: *which 80%?*

Not "how do I use AI for teaching". Too big. Not "can AI plan my whole week". Wrong scoping. The right scope is one task at a time, named, with a finite output.

**Bad scope:** "Help me prepare for next week."
**Good scope:** "Draft 8 short-answer questions on Class 9 ICSE Civics chapter 3, with a 2-mark and 4-mark mix, for a Friday quiz."

The smaller the scope, the better the AI does. The smaller the scope, the easier *you* can verify the output. Both move in the same direction. This is one of the few free wins in the whole field.

blocks.title: Translation: from a vague Sunday-night thought to a real prompt

steps.label: Step 1 — The Sunday thought
steps.body: "Ugh, I have to teach the Periodic Table on Tuesday." Not yet a prompt. It's a feeling.

steps.label: Step 2 — Identify the audience
steps.body: Class 9 CBSE, mixed-ability section, 38 students. Last year's class found atomic mass confusing. That's audience-specific signal AI doesn't know.

steps.label: Step 3 — Identify the outcome
steps.body: By the end of the period, students should be able to read a periodic-table cell and tell you the element's atomic number, mass, and group. That's three concrete verbs, not a vibe.

steps.label: Step 4 — Identify the time and constraint
steps.body: 40-minute period, no lab access, board + chalk + textbook only. AI doesn't know the lab is locked on Tuesdays.

steps.label: Step 5 — Write the prompt
steps.body: "Draft a 40-minute lesson plan for Class 9 CBSE Science (mixed-ability, 38 students, no lab) so that by the end students can read a periodic-table cell and identify atomic number, atomic mass, and group. Open with a 3-minute hook. Include one quick check-for-understanding at minute 25."

steps.label: Step 6 — Read what came back
steps.body: First draft is 70% useful. You'll cut the cheesy hook, replace the example, keep the structure. 12 minutes saved on a task that used to take 35.

blocks.prompt: You're prepping a Class 7 English class on figurative language for tomorrow. Which prompt is best-scoped for a first try?

choices.label: "Help me with figurative language."
choices.explain: No grade, no time, no outcome, no class context. AI will give you a Wikipedia-flavoured general answer.

choices.label: "Draft a 35-minute Class 7 English lesson on simile and metaphor with one 5-minute group activity, ending with 4 quick-check MCQs. Indian-context examples preferred."
choices.explain: Scope, time, outcome, format, locale. AI now has enough to produce something class-ready.

choices.label: "Make my class more engaging."
choices.explain: An adjective is not a brief. "Engaging" is your job; structure and timing are the AI's.

choices.label: "Just give me everything you know about metaphors."
choices.explain: Information dump request. You'll get a wall of text that takes longer to read than to write the lesson yourself.

hi-IN.title: Sunday raat, 9:42 PM
hi-IN.md:
Tu Sunday ko 9:42 PM pe ChatGPT khol ke likhta hai: "plan my week." Phir 11:30 PM tak prompts iterate kar raha hai, paani peeke, jhunjhlaake, finally Word document ban gaya — *aur Monday ko subah dekha to wahi pranayama-shanti-OM jaisa generic plan hai.*

Galati AI ki nahi. Tune brief hi nahi diya. Bhej diya "plan my week" — Anand Mahindra bhi itni vague request pe team se kuch nahi nikaal sakta.

en.title: Sunday night, 9:42 PM
en.md: You open ChatGPT at 9:42 PM, type "plan my week," and at 11:30 PM you have a generic-sounding document that could belong to anyone teaching anything. The AI didn't fail. Your brief did. "Plan my week" is not a brief; it's a sigh.

blocks.text: Move 2 — AI grades the rough, you grade the meaning

blocks.md:
There is one move that, if you only learn one move from this entire course, will keep you out of trouble: **AI grades the rough, you grade the meaning.**

AI is good at structure. Is the paragraph well-formed? Is the grammar tight? Is the spelling right? Is the rubric checklist met? Yes, yes, yes. AI does these in seconds.

AI is bad at meaning. Did the child *understand*? Is this argument actually true? Has the student answered the *question* or just the prompt-shaped hole around it? AI cannot tell you this reliably. It can guess; it will guess fluently; it will sometimes be confidently wrong, and "confidently wrong" is the worst possible failure mode in grading.

Use AI for the rough check (structure). Use yourself for the meaning check. Never reverse the order.

coach.name: Principal Priya
coach.role: Your principal, 22 years on the floor, low patience for jargon

intro: Priya pulls a chair next to yours in the staff room.
"Five quick scenarios. Tell me — boring 80% (AI handles it) or human 20% (you handle it)? I just want to know if you can tell the difference."

scenarios.situation: Ananya's grandmother passed away last week. You need to write her a short note acknowledging her return to class.
scenarios.explain: Human 20%. AI can produce technically polite words. The child needs to feel that *you* noticed; outsourced sympathy reads exactly as outsourced.

scenarios.situation: Drafting 12 multiple-choice questions on the structure of a plant cell for tomorrow's Class 8 quiz.
scenarios.explain: Boring 80%. AI does this fast and cleanly. You read them, drop the bad ones, fix the keys. 5-minute task instead of a 25-minute one.

scenarios.situation: Aarav slept through your class three days running. You suspect something at home but you don't know what.
scenarios.explain: Human 20%. AI cannot have the conversation that finds out. It can draft a parent email *after* the conversation; it can't replace the conversation.

scenarios.situation: Reformatting last year's Class 11 Physics paper into the new CBSE blueprint format.
scenarios.explain: Boring 80%. Pure structure shuffling. AI handles it well; you spot-check the section weights.

scenarios.situation: Writing the nuanced descriptive comment on Riya's report card that has to acknowledge real progress and a real ongoing weakness without being either falsely cheery or harsh.
scenarios.explain: Human 20%. AI will give you a fine *first* draft to start from — but the calibration of tone, the specific incident you reference, that's yours. The parent reading it can tell.

scenarios.situation: Generating a one-page summary of the NCERT chapter on Mughal architecture for an absent student.
scenarios.explain: Boring 80%. AI summarises textbook content well; you skim once for accuracy and add one sentence pointing to the key paragraph she should still read herself.

blocks.title: The classic trap: letting AI grade essays unsupervised
blocks.md:
It is so tempting. 30 essays, AI scores them all in 4 minutes, you post the marks. Don't.

AI is a fluent reader of *form*. It cannot reliably tell whether the argument is true, whether the example actually supports the claim, whether the conclusion follows. It will mark a polished, wrong essay higher than a rough, brilliant one.

Use AI to give you a *reading order* (start with the ones it scored highest and lowest, calibrate your eye, then sample the middle). Never as the final mark. Marks of record are the human 20%.

blocks.prompt: Order these steps the way a disciplined teacher uses AI for end-of-unit essays.

items.label: Decide the rubric yourself
items.detail: What you're actually grading for, before AI sees the work.

items.label: Have AI score essays against the rubric
items.detail: Triage only — produces a reading order, not marks.

items.label: Read the top-and-bottom-scored essays first
items.detail: Calibrate your eye against the AI's structure read.

items.label: Sample 5 from the middle band
items.detail: This is where AI structure ≠ meaning shows up.

items.label: Mark every essay yourself with AI score visible but ignored when you disagree
items.detail: AI is the second opinion; you are the grader of record.

items.label: Post the marks with feedback you wrote
items.detail: Voice is yours; structure can be AI-assisted; meaning is yours.

blocks.hint: Rubric first, AI as triage, your read decides.

blocks.instruction: Pick one task on your plate this week. Write *your* version of a brief for it — audience, time, outcome, constraint, format. Five lines, no more.
blocks.starter:
Audience: 
Time: 
Outcome (what students should be able to do at the end): 
Constraint (anything AI doesn't know): 
Format (what should the AI hand back):
blocks.expected:
Audience: Class 9 CBSE Science, mixed-ability, 38 students, period 4 (just after lunch — they're sleepy)
Time: 35 minutes (5 minutes of attendance + transition first)
Outcome: students should be able to identify exothermic vs endothermic reactions and give one example of each
Constraint: no lab access, no projector this period, board + chalk only
Format: a 35-minute lesson plan with a timed schedule, plus 4 exit-ticket questions

blocks.prompt: Pick the situations where the boring/human line is being held *correctly*.

choices.label: You used AI to draft 8 quiz questions, picked 5, edited 2, wrote one yourself.
choices.explain: Textbook good use. AI is doing the drafting; you're doing the curation. Both lanes intact.

choices.label: You used AI to write the eulogy at a school memorial assembly, with light edits.
choices.explain: Wrong lane. A memorial is the human 20%. The students will know — they always know.

choices.label: You used AI to summarise the NCERT chapter for an absent student, then added a personal sentence at the end.
choices.explain: Boring 80% with a human touch on top. Cheap, kind, defensible.

choices.label: You used AI to grade descriptive answers and posted marks without reading the essays.
choices.explain: Reverses the model. AI grades structure, you grade meaning. Posting AI marks unread is the failure mode this whole lesson is about.

hi-IN.title: VIVA scene, real story
hi-IN.md:
Class 12 Physics, viva tha. Bachche ne ChatGPT se *script* yaad ki — ek baar examiner ne side question maara: "is se pehle kya step kiya tha?" Bachcha frozen. Memory expired. ChatGPT reload nahi kar sakta tha viva room mein.

Matlab dekh — *bachche* ki galti kam thi; *teacher* ki galti badi thi, ki viva ka structure aisa hi tha jo sirf rote answer test karta hai. Honest assessment design hota to AI ka shortcut kaam hi nahi karta.

en.title: The viva that wasn't
en.md: A Class 12 student memorises a ChatGPT-written viva script. The examiner asks one off-script follow-up. The student freezes. The fault is not entirely the student's; the viva format was a recall test wearing a viva costume. The honest design lives in the next lessons.

blocks.title: Field Notes: The Photosynthesis A-Grade
blocks.source: Anonymous senior English teacher at a CBSE-affiliated school in Bandra, Mumbai
blocks.story:
On October 7, 2024, a Grade 12 English teacher in Mumbai uploaded **63 board-prep essays** to an AI grading tool over a weekend. She had a JEE-prep daughter, a sick mother-in-law, and a Diwali break starting Tuesday. The tool returned grades and feedback in 41 minutes. She copy-pasted the marks into the school portal without reading a single rubric.

One essay, by a quiet Marathi-medium student named Rohan, scored a glowing **A (92/100)**. The essay was on "The Role of Sunlight in Modern Civilization" and contained the sentence: *"Photosynthesis primarily occurs in the mitochondria of plant cells, releasing oxygen as a byproduct."* The AI praised it for "strong scientific grounding."

Rohan's father, a retired botanist, read the graded essay over Diwali sweets. He was, charitably, unimpressed. The complaint reached the principal on October 14. By October 22, the school auditor had pulled all **47 essays** the teacher had graded that weekend; **9 contained factual errors the AI had rewarded**. Every grade was reissued. Two parents threatened to escalate to the CBSE board. The teacher kept her job but lost her Class 12 section for the following year.

She later told the auditor: *"I trusted it because the marks looked reasonable. I forgot a reasonable-looking mark and a correct mark are not the same thing."*
blocks.takeaway: AI grades fluently, not accurately. Fluency without a teacher's eye is just confident wrong-ness, served fast.

blocks.title: Boss Battle: Sunday 11pm, 38 Essays, One Cup of Chai
blocks.setup:
It's **Sunday, 11:14pm**. You're **Ms. Anjali**, government school teacher in Pune, 15 years in the trade, **Day 6** of your principal-approved "AI in my classroom" 90-day pilot. Tomorrow at 9am, **38 Class 10 history essays** on the Quit India Movement are due back to students. You've graded six. Your back hurts.

The AI tool — paid for from a ₹47,000 annual school budget you fought hard for — can grade the rest in twelve minutes. The dashboard is open. The "Grade All" button is glowing. Your daughter has a Marathi unit test tomorrow and you promised to revise with her.

Your mentor pings you on WhatsApp: *"Anjali, before you click anything, talk to me."*

coach.name: Mentor-Master Mukherjee
coach.role: Retired DIET faculty, 32 years training teachers, your AI-pilot guide

stages.prompt: Mukherjee asks: *"What's the actual job AI is doing here, in one sentence?"* What do you tell yourself before you click anything?

options.label: "AI is grading my essays so I don't have to."
options.explain: This is the framing that produced the Bandra photosynthesis incident. If AI is *replacing* your judgment, you've outsourced the one thing parents and the board are paying you to do. Mukherjee groans audibly over the phone.

options.label: "AI is doing a first-pass scoring; I'm doing the final grade."
options.explain: **Yes.** This is the assistant frame, not the replacement frame. AI handles volume; you handle judgment. The pilot is meant to save you 60% of the time, not 100% of the responsibility.

options.label: "AI is faster than me, so its grade is probably more consistent."
options.explain: Consistency is not accuracy. An AI can be perfectly consistent at being subtly wrong about the Quit India Movement (it once told a Delhi teacher Gandhi led the 1857 revolt). Mukherjee asks you to put the chai down and read the rubric.

options.label: "AI is a draft I review; the grade in the portal is mine, with my name on it."
options.explain: **The strongest framing.** Your name goes in the school register, not the AI's. If a parent escalates on Tuesday, "the AI graded it" is not a defence the principal will accept. Own the output, use the assist.

stages.prompt: OK. You'll AI-grade, then review. **How do you set up the pass to make review actually possible** at 11:30pm on a Sunday?

options.label: Click "Grade All," wait 12 minutes, copy-paste 38 grades into the portal, sleep.
options.explain: This is the Bandra Sunday on rerun. "Review" that happens after grades are in the portal isn't review; it's archaeology. By the time you spot an error, the student has already seen the grade.

options.label: AI-grade all 38, then spot-check **6 random essays** before publishing any grade.
options.explain: **Practical.** A 6-essay spot-check (16% sample) catches systematic errors — if the AI is misreading the Quit India dates in two of six, you know to slow down on all 38. Random beats top-3, top-3 introduces bias.

options.label: AI-grade, then read **only the A-grade and F-grade essays**; trust the middle.
options.explain: Half-credit. The extremes are where parents complain, so you're not crazy. But Rohan's photosynthesis A would have been caught by this method only because his father is a botanist. The middle is where systematic errors hide; you can't trust the middle without sampling it.

options.label: AI-grade tonight, but **publish nothing until Monday morning** after a 30-minute fresh-eye review.
options.explain: **Strongest move.** Sunday 11pm fatigue + AI fluency = the photosynthesis trap. Sleep, drink coffee, do the spot-check at 7am with a clear head. Mukherjee approves; he says he wishes more teachers separated *generation* from *publication*.

stages.prompt: AI returns the grades. Spot-check time. **Essay #14** scored 88/100 — high A. The AI feedback says: *"Strong grasp of historical context, especially the role of Subhash Chandra Bose in launching the Quit India Movement in 1942."* What do you do?

options.label: Looks reasonable. Move on. Bose was important in that era.
options.explain: **This is the moment Rohan's father caught.** Subhash Chandra Bose did not launch the Quit India Movement — Gandhi did, with the August 8, 1942 Bombay session of the AICC. Bose was already abroad founding the INA. The AI is fluently, confidently wrong, and you just rewarded the student for it.

options.label: Open the essay. Read it. Cross-check the AI's claim against the rubric.
options.explain: **Yes.** You read the essay; the student didn't actually write that Bose launched Quit India — the AI hallucinated the praise. The student's actual work is solid. You revise the feedback, keep the grade close, and flag the AI's confabulation in your pilot log.

options.label: Lower the grade by 10 points to be safe — "if I'm not sure, the student loses."
options.explain: You're now punishing the student for the AI's error. That's worse than trusting the AI; it's compounding the AI's mistake with your fear. Mukherjee says "chhi chhi" loud enough that you hear it through the phone.

options.label: Flag this essay for tomorrow morning's full re-grade by hand, ungraded for now.
options.explain: **Solid.** When the AI's feedback contains a verifiable factual claim that you can't immediately confirm, the right move is to defer, not to publish. One ungraded essay returned Tuesday is much cheaper than 47 reissued grades like Bandra.

stages.prompt: Last call. You finish the spot-check at 12:08am. **2 of 6 essays had AI feedback errors** (33% error rate in the sample). What do you do with the remaining 32 essays?

options.label: Publish all 38. The errors I found were minor.
options.explain: 33% sample error rate projects to roughly 10-12 wrong essays in the full set. Publishing now is the Bandra script with different names. Mukherjee texts: *"If you publish, I won't be your mentor anymore. Half-joking."*

options.label: Publish the 4 clean ones from the sample. Hand-grade the other 34 myself this week.
options.explain: **Honest move.** You salvage what's verified, you do the work for the rest, and you tell the class on Monday: *"Some grades are out today, the rest by Friday — I'm checking each one carefully."* Students respect transparency; principals reward it.

options.label: Re-run the AI with a stricter prompt and hope for fewer errors.
options.explain: You don't know whether the prompt was the problem or the model is just confidently wrong about Indian history. Re-running without diagnosing is gambling, and you have a 90-day pilot to defend.

options.label: Pause publication, log the 33% error rate in your pilot notebook, escalate to Mukherjee Monday.
options.explain: **Pilot-grade thinking.** A 33% AI-feedback error rate in Week 1 is the most important data you'll collect this quarter. Document it; it's the difference between a pilot that gets renewed and one that gets quietly killed.

outcomes.perfect: Day 6 of the pilot and you've already learned the lesson Bandra learned in October. You used AI as an assistant, not a replacement; you separated generation from publication; you caught a confabulated Bose claim that would have ended up in 38 student notebooks. **Mukherjee sends you a single emoji: a folded-hands namaste.** Sleep well.
outcomes.good: You avoided the headline disaster, mostly. Re-read the lesson on the **assistant frame** — the difference between "AI graded it" and "AI helped me grade it" is the difference between a 90-day pilot that succeeds and one that becomes a cautionary slide in next year's CBSE conference.
outcomes.learn: You let fluency stand in for accuracy, which is exactly what the Bandra teacher did. Re-read this lesson, especially the section on **why AI feedback can be confidently wrong about Indian history** and the **3-step assistant protocol**. Mukherjee will be available again on Wednesday; bring your pilot notebook.

points: Teaching is two jobs: the boring 80% (structure work AI does well) and the human 20% (judgment work AI does badly). Drawing the line is the whole skill.
AI is a fluent intern who has never met your students. Trust it accordingly.
Scope every task before opening the AI; the smaller the brief, the better the output.
AI grades the rough, you grade the meaning. Never reverse the order on marks of record.
Letting AI grade unread is the classic trap. Use it for reading order, not for the marks themselves.

blocks.prompt: Pick one task you did this week that you spent more than 30 minutes on. Was it boring 80% or human 20%? If it was boring 80%, why didn't you delegate it?

lessons.title: Lesson Prep That Actually Saves Time
lessons.subtitle: Brief AI like you'd brief a student teacher

audioChapters.label: Opening — why most AI prep saves zero minutes

blocks.md:
Here is the dirty secret of teacher AI use. Most teachers who say "AI saves me hours" are actually saving *minutes*, and losing the rest in iteration. They paste in something vague, get back something vague, edit, re-prompt, edit again, and end up with a worksheet that is technically a worksheet but isn't actually class-ready.

The difference between a 10-minute prep and a 35-minute prep isn't the AI; it's the brief you put in front of it. This lesson gives you the brief structure, the two moves that get you to a usable first draft, and the named trap that swallows most teachers' Tuesday evening.

blocks.title: Mental model: brief AI like you'd brief a student teacher who flies in tomorrow
blocks.md:
Imagine a student teacher arriving at 7 AM Tuesday to deliver your second period. You have one WhatsApp message worth of words to brief them with before they walk in.

You would *never* write "teach photosynthesis." You'd write: *Class 7, 35 kids, 40-minute period, mixed ability, no projector, end with a 4-question exit ticket, the kids already know the leaf parts so don't restart there.* Five lines. Specific.

That is the brief AI deserves. Same five lines, same specificity. Anything less and you're sending a half-trained intern to teach Class 7 with a vibe.

blocks.caption: Build the brief one line at a time and watch the lesson plan output sharpen.

hi-IN.title: Tiffin instructions, lesson plan instructions
hi-IN.md:
Tu apni saasu maa ko bolta hai "khaana bana do" — kya milega? Jo unko theek lage. Aalu paratha bhi ho sakta hai, sago khichdi bhi, kuch bhi.

Lekin jab tu bolta hai "thoda kam tel mein, raat ka bachcha hai isliye light, dahi side mein, 7 baje tak" — *uss* level pe khana milta hai jo actually khaaya jaata hai.

AI ka prompt bhi waisa hi hai. Vague maango, vague milega. Specific maango, kaam ka milega. Saasu maa AI se zyaada patient hai shayad — par AI session zyaada cheap hai.

en.title: Same point, no Hinglish
en.md: If you ask anyone "make me food," you get whatever they feel like making. If you ask for "low oil, light dinner, ready by 7," you get something you can actually eat. AI prompts work the same way.

blocks.md:
Most teachers' AI prompts start with the *topic* ("photosynthesis"). The good ones start with the *outcome* ("by the end, students should be able to label inputs and outputs of photosynthesis on a leaf diagram").

This seems like a small reordering. It is not. Outcome-first prompts force you to know what success looks like *before* you ask AI for the path. AI is good at finding paths to specified destinations and very bad at picking destinations on your behalf.

The magic phrase: **"By the end of the period, students should be able to ____"** — fill in *one* concrete verb. Then ask AI for the lesson.

blocks.title: Translation: from a topic in your head to a prompt that returns a class-ready plan

steps.label: Step 1 — Resist the topic
steps.body: You think "I have to teach the French Revolution." That is a topic. AI can do anything with a topic, which means it does nothing useful with a topic.

steps.label: Step 2 — Pick the outcome verb
steps.body: What should students be able to *do* at the end? Not "understand the French Revolution" (untestable). Try: *explain what 'liberty, equality, fraternity' looked like to a 1789 Parisian baker*. Concrete. Testable in one paragraph.

steps.label: Step 3 — Add the audience and constraint
steps.body: Class 9 ICSE, 38 students, 35-minute period, no projector. The baker example will land harder than the Robespierre name-drop.

steps.label: Step 4 — Add the format you want back
steps.body: "Hand back: a timed lesson outline, one primary-source extract under 80 words, three quick-check questions at the end." Format spec keeps AI from giving you 8 paragraphs of prose you don't have time to read.

steps.label: Step 5 — Read the draft, then iterate once
steps.body: First draft will have one weak section. Don't redo the whole prompt. Say: "replace the hook with one tied to a present-day Indian protest students will recognise." Targeted edit.

steps.label: Step 6 — Stop iterating
steps.body: Two iterations is the budget. After two, you're polishing fingerprints. Print it, walk in, teach. Quality threshold: would a junior colleague find it usable? Yes? Done.

blocks.prompt: You're prepping a Class 10 Civics class on the structure of Indian Parliament. Which prompt is *outcome-first*?

choices.label: "Make a lesson on the Indian Parliament for Class 10."
choices.explain: Topic-first. "Indian Parliament" can be approached six ways; AI will pick a default that may not match yours.

choices.label: "By the end of a 40-minute period, my Class 10 CBSE students should be able to label Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha, and the President's role on a one-page diagram. Plan the period."
choices.explain: Outcome-first. The destination is named in concrete verbs; AI now produces a plan that gets students there.

choices.label: "Cover everything important about Parliament."
choices.explain: "Important" is undefined. Whose definition? AI's, which means generic.

choices.label: "Make the Parliament lesson exciting."
choices.explain: Adjective without scaffolding. Excitement is your job; structure is the AI's.

hi-IN.title: B.Ed se sikha tha, ab phir kaam aaya
hi-IN.md:
B.Ed mein "learning outcome" likhwaate the. Tu rolling eyes maar ke likhta tha "students will be able to demonstrate understanding" — bekaar, generic, sab class mein chal jaata.

Ab jab AI ko brief karta hai, woh hi exact training kaam aati hai. *Concrete verb*: identify, label, calculate, list, contrast. Generic verb: understand, appreciate, learn. Generic verb daala to AI generic plan dega; concrete verb daala to AI concrete plan dega. Bachpan ki training kaam aa gayi — late, but on time.

en.title: B.Ed coming back to help
en.md: Remember writing "students will be able to demonstrate understanding" in your B.Ed assignments and rolling your eyes? Concrete verbs — identify, label, calculate, contrast — were the actual point. Now AI is the audience that finally rewards you for using them.

blocks.text: Move 2 — The 'rewrite for class X' move

blocks.md:
Here is a tiny, specific move that pays for itself within an hour: **the 'rewrite for class X' move.**

You wrote a beautiful Class 10 lesson plan last year. This year you have a Class 8 section and a Class 11 section. Both need adapted versions of the same content. Don't replan from scratch.

Paste your Class 10 plan into AI and say: *"Rewrite this for Class 8 — same outcome, more concrete examples, simpler language, shorter paragraphs."* Then: *"Now rewrite for Class 11 — same outcome, add one challenging extension question, allow more independent work."*

You now have three plans in 15 minutes. The original is yours; the variants are AI-assisted. None are generic, because the *original* wasn't.

coach.name: Principal Priya
coach.role: Your principal, dropping in between class observations

intro: Priya holds out her phone with five teachers' AI prompts on it.
"Quick. Tell me which of these will produce a usable lesson on the first try, and which is going to waste an hour."

scenarios.situation: "Plan a Class 8 Hindi lesson on Premchand."
scenarios.explain: No outcome, no time, no specific story or theme, no constraint. AI will give you a four-page essay that takes longer to read than to ignore.

scenarios.situation: "By the end of a 35-minute period, my Class 8 ICSE Hindi students should be able to identify three social ironies in *Idgah*. Plan the period with a 5-minute opening hook, a 15-minute close-reading activity, and 4 exit questions."
scenarios.explain: Outcome, time, format, scaffolding — all present. AI returns something you can teach from with two edits.

scenarios.situation: "Make the Periodic Table fun for Class 9."
scenarios.explain: "Fun" is your job. AI will give you fake-sounding analogies that the class will see through. "Fun" is a result, not an instruction.

scenarios.situation: "Take this Class 10 Maths lesson plan I wrote last year [paste]. Rewrite for a Class 8 section: same outcome (graphing linear equations), simpler examples, more guided practice."
scenarios.explain: Anchored in your own existing work, with concrete delta instructions. AI does best when it's editing, not inventing.

scenarios.situation: "Give me 12 multiple-choice questions on Class 11 Economics chapter 5, mixed difficulty: 4 easy/recall, 6 medium/application, 2 hard/synthesis. Indian context examples preferred."
scenarios.explain: Specific count, specific difficulty distribution, specific context. AI delivers; you cull and edit.

scenarios.situation: "Just give me everything important about the Mughal era for Class 7."
scenarios.explain: "Everything important" is undefined. AI's default for that prompt is a Wikipedia summary; you'll spend 25 minutes editing structure that should have been in the brief.

blocks.caption: Watch the trap happen live — and the fix at the end.

blocks.title: The classic trap: the generic-worksheet-from-generic-prompt loop
blocks.md:
You write "give me a worksheet on integers." AI returns a passable, generic worksheet. You print it. You walk into class. You realise the worksheet doesn't match what your kids actually struggled with last week. You write another vague prompt. Repeat.

The trap is *not* that AI is bad. The trap is that vague prompts produce average outputs, and average outputs are *just good enough* to print, which means you never push yourself to write a real brief.

The fix is mechanical: never paste a prompt under 50 words for a non-trivial task. If your prompt is shorter than that, you haven't briefed it; you've sighed at it.

blocks.prompt: Order these steps the way an efficient teacher writes a lesson prep prompt.

items.label: Identify the audience (class, board, section size)
items.detail: AI doesn't know your second-period section is louder than your fourth.

items.label: Pick one concrete outcome verb
items.detail: Identify, label, calculate, contrast — not understand, appreciate, learn.

items.label: State the time and physical constraint
items.detail: 40 minutes, no projector, board only — AI cannot guess this.

items.label: Specify the format you want back
items.detail: Lesson outline + 4 exit questions, not 'a comprehensive plan'.

items.label: Add one local context anchor
items.detail: Pune flooding example, JEE practice problem style, Hindi-medium friendly.

items.label: Send and read the draft once before iterating
items.detail: First draft is ~70%. Edit once with targeted feedback, then stop.

blocks.hint: Audience, outcome, time, format, context, send. The order keeps you honest.

blocks.instruction: Pick a topic you teach next week. Write a real, structured prompt for it — 50+ words. Do not skip any of the six brief lines.
blocks.starter:
Audience (class, board, size, anything AI can't guess): 
Outcome (concrete verb, what students do at the end): 
Time + constraints: 
Format I want back: 
Local context to use: 
Send (read once, edit once, then stop):
blocks.expected:
Audience: Class 10 CBSE Maths, 42 students, mixed ability, the 'after-PT' period (lower energy)
Outcome: students should be able to identify when a quadratic equation has two real roots, one repeated root, or no real roots, by computing the discriminant
Time + constraints: 45 minutes, board + chalk, 5 students typically need extra walkthrough
Format I want back: a 45-minute timed plan, 3 worked examples (one of each discriminant case), 6 practice questions of mixed difficulty, 1 exit-ticket question
Local context to use: JEE-Main style stem framing for the practice questions; mention the discriminant as 'D' (kids see it that way in Hindi-medium board notes too)
Send (read once, edit once, then stop): plan to iterate only once — replace the weak example with one I write myself

blocks.prompt: Pick the prep practices that *actually* save time in week one of using AI.

choices.label: Reuse your own old lesson plans as the seed and ask AI to rewrite for a different class
choices.explain: Highest leverage move. Your originals are anchored in your students; AI just remixes.

choices.label: Build a 6-line brief template and reuse it for every prompt this term
choices.explain: Yes. Templates are how you skip the Sunday-night iteration spiral. Audience, outcome, time, format, context, send.

choices.label: Always start from a fresh prompt for variety
choices.explain: This is how teachers reset to vague prompts and lose time. Variety is good in *examples*, not in *prompt structure*.

choices.label: Iterate with the AI five times until the plan is exactly right
choices.explain: Two iterations is the budget. After that, you're polishing fingerprints AI can't see anyway. Open the plan in Word and finish by hand.

hi-IN.title: Marathi-medium school, Pune
hi-IN.md:
Sneha ma'am, Marathi-medium school mein, ChatGPT bole 'plan kar de' — ChatGPT ne Marathi mein plan diya, par 'पाठ' aur 'धडा' confuse kar gaya, sab gadbad. Sneha ma'am ne 25 min lagaake fix kiya.

Next din strategy badli: ChatGPT ko English mein structure puchha (outline, question stems, rubric), Marathi version *khud* likha. 12 minute mein ho gaya. Aur acha bhi tha — kyunki language layer Sneha ma'am ke paas thi, structure layer AI ke paas. Apna apna kaam.

en.title: Marathi-medium reality
en.md: AI's Indian-language output is uneven. The fix is to ask AI for the *structure* (outline, question stems, rubric) in English and translate yourself. Faster, cleaner, and the local fluency stays where it belongs — with you.

blocks.title: Field Notes: From 4 Hours to 45 Minutes (Once She Wrote the Brief)
blocks.source: Anonymous Class 9 Science teacher at a Pune Municipal Corporation school, 11 years experience
blocks.story:
On January 3, 2025, a science teacher in Pune ran her first "brief-first" AI prep session. Until December, she had been spending **4 hours every Sunday** writing weekly lesson plans for her two Class 9 sections — one English-medium, one Marathi-medium, both heterogeneous, with a 4-grade-level reading spread between her strongest and weakest students.

Her first six attempts at AI prep had been disasters. She'd type *"give me a lesson plan on chemical reactions"* and get back generic American-curriculum content with experiments her school's lab couldn't run. She'd spend 2 hours fixing it and 2 more hours rewriting it. Net savings: zero.

The shift came when a colleague made her write a **one-page class brief** before opening the AI tool: 32 students, ages 13-14, Maharashtra State Board syllabus, Marathi-medium, no Bunsen burners (gas line broken since November), reading levels Class 5 to Class 9, exam in 18 days, last week's quiz showed 70% confused acids and bases.

With the brief pasted as the *first message*, the AI's output went from "unusable" to "80% shippable." Her Sunday prep dropped to **45 minutes**. Across one semester she logged a **47% reduction** in total prep time and reused the same brief (lightly edited) for 14 weeks.

The brief was the unlock. The model was the same model her colleagues were complaining about.
blocks.takeaway: AI prep doesn't fail because the model is bad. It fails because the teacher hasn't written down who their students actually are.

blocks.title: Boss Battle: The Heterogeneous Class 9 and the Sunday Brief
blocks.setup:
**Sunday, 3pm. Day 19** of your AI pilot. You're **Ms. Anjali**, and last week's prep took **3 hours 40 minutes** even with the AI — the output was generic, you rewrote half of it, and your Class 9 section walked out confused about ionic bonds. Mukherjee told you on Friday: *"You're treating the AI like a search engine. Treat it like a substitute teacher who's never met your kids. Brief it."*

You've opened a blank document titled `class-9-brief.md`. Your class is: **34 students, ages 13-15, Maharashtra State Board, Marathi-medium with English science textbooks, 6 students reading at Class 6 level, 4 students writing JEE Foundation prep on the side, broken lab gas line, term-end exam in 22 days.** Mukherjee is on a video call with you, sipping cutting chai, ready to review your brief before you write a single prompt.

coach.name: Mentor-Master Mukherjee
coach.role: Retired DIET faculty, 32 years training teachers, your AI-pilot guide

stages.prompt: Mukherjee asks: *"Before we write the brief, what is the brief actually for?"* What's the right answer?

options.label: It's a one-page document I paste at the start of every prep session so the AI knows my class.
options.explain: **Yes.** The brief is a *reusable context primer*. You write it once, edit it monthly, paste it as Message 1 of every prep session for the rest of the semester. It saves you from re-explaining 34 students every Sunday.

options.label: It's a list of every topic in the syllabus.
options.explain: That's the syllabus. The brief is about the *students*, not the curriculum. The syllabus is in the textbook; the brief is what the textbook can't tell the AI.

options.label: It's a backup for when the AI gives me bad output, so I have something to fall back on.
options.explain: Backwards. The brief is what *prevents* bad output, not what salvages it. Mukherjee makes a tutting sound.

options.label: It's the answer to: "What does the AI need to know about my class that the syllabus doesn't tell it?"
options.explain: **Strongest framing.** Reading levels, language medium, lab constraints, last quiz's confusions, the JEE-prep kids in row 3 — none of that is in the syllabus, and all of it changes what "a good lesson on ionic bonds" actually means.

stages.prompt: OK. You start drafting. Which **four facts** must go in the brief? (Pick the strongest single answer.)

options.label: Topic, learning objective, time available, materials in the lab.
options.explain: These are fine, but they're all about *the lesson*, not *the students*. The Bandra teachers had this; their AI output was still generic. The brief's edge comes from student facts.

options.label: Class size, age range, language medium, the spread of reading/skill levels.
options.explain: **This is the unlock.** A lesson for 34 mixed-ability Marathi-medium kids is structurally different from a lesson for 22 English-medium high-performers. The Pune teacher's 47% time saving came from getting the AI to stop assuming American Honors Chem.

options.label: The full syllabus PDF, the school's mission statement, and the exam timetable.
options.explain: You'll burn the AI's context window on documents it doesn't need to read. A 600-page syllabus PDF crowds out the 6 sentences that actually shape the lesson.

options.label: Constraints (broken gas line, no projector), the last assessment's confusions, what's coming up (exam in 22 days), the medium of instruction.
options.explain: **Even stronger.** Constraints (no Bunsen burner) prevent the AI from suggesting experiments you can't run. Last quiz's confusions (acids vs bases) tell it what to reinforce. Together they collapse the AI's option space to lessons that *fit your room*.

stages.prompt: You write the brief. **312 words.** Mukherjee reads it. He says: *"One thing missing — the part the AI will most want to skip."* What did you forget?

options.label: The exam syllabus chapter list.
options.explain: Important, but not the missing piece. The AI doesn't *skip* this; it just doesn't differentiate between "in syllabus" and "deeply in syllabus."

options.label: The names of the JEE-prep students so the AI can address them by name.
options.explain: Don't put student names in an AI prompt. PII, consent, data retention — none of those conversations have happened with parents in your pilot agreement. Mukherjee shakes his head firmly.

options.label: The 6 students reading at Class 6 level and what "differentiation" means for them.
options.explain: **Yes.** AI tools, untreated, write to the median. Without explicit instruction to provide a Class-6-readable variant of each activity, the bottom 6 students get a lesson they can't access — and you spend Monday afternoon reteaching from scratch. The brief must say: *"Provide a simplified-language version of each activity for the 6 students at Class 6 reading level."*

options.label: A worked example of what "good output" looks like for me — i.e., one past lesson I was happy with.
options.explain: **Excellent.** A single "this is the kind of lesson I want" example does more than three paragraphs of instruction. The AI calibrates to your taste. Mukherjee calls this the *show, don't tell* principle of prompting.

stages.prompt: Brief is ready. You paste it, then write your first prompt: *"Plan a 40-minute lesson on ionic bonds."* The AI returns a draft. **What do you check first?**

options.label: Whether the lesson is exactly 40 minutes.
options.explain: Time-fit matters but it's the easiest thing to fix. Check the load-bearing constraints first — the ones that, if wrong, mean the whole lesson is unusable.

options.label: Whether any activity requires the broken gas line / Bunsen burner.
options.explain: **Hard constraint check.** If the AI ignored your "no Bunsen burner" line, you've learned something important about how this model handles your brief — and you fix the prompt, not the lesson. The Pune teacher caught this on her first run and it changed her workflow.

options.label: Whether the differentiation for the 6 lower-reading-level students is actually present.
options.explain: **Yes.** This is the load-bearing piece you specifically added to the brief. If the AI omitted it (or hand-waved "adapt as needed"), the brief failed to land and you need to push back: *"Show me the simplified-language version explicitly."*

options.label: Whether the lesson is in Marathi.
options.explain: You said Marathi-medium *with English science textbooks* in the brief — so the lesson plan in English is correct. Mukherjee gently suggests you re-read your own brief.

outcomes.perfect: You wrote a brief that names the students, the constraints, the gaps, and the standard of "good." Sunday prep just dropped from 3h40m to about an hour and the lesson actually fits your classroom. **Mukherjee texts: *"Save this brief. Reuse it for 14 weeks. Edit it once a month."*** That's the whole methodology.
outcomes.good: You got most of the brief right. The differentiation piece or the constraints piece slipped — and that's the difference between an 80% shippable draft and 50%. Re-read the lesson on the **brief-first protocol** and look at the worked example. Try again next Sunday.
outcomes.learn: You're still in the "AI as search engine" mode that cost you 4 hours last week. Re-read the lesson, especially the section on **the four facts that change everything** and **why student-facts beat lesson-facts**. The 47% time saving is real, but only after the brief is written. Until then, it's just a frustrating chatbot.

points: Brief AI like a student teacher arriving at 7 AM: audience, outcome, time, format, constraint, context. Five-line brief; 50-word minimum.
Outcome-first beats topic-first. Pick one concrete verb (label, identify, contrast) before you open the AI window.
Reuse your own old plans as the seed. AI is a much better editor than inventor; your originals are the only thing AI can't fake.
Two iterations is the iteration budget. After that, finish by hand.
Generic prompts produce average outputs that are just good enough to print — and that's the trap. 50-word minimum keeps you honest.

audioChapters.label: Mental model: rubrics are the AI's superpower
Move 1 — AI-drafted feedback you actually review

blocks.md:
It is Sunday at 9 PM. Thirty Class 11 essays sit on your desk. You have not opened them. Your phone says you have promised to send marks tomorrow.

AI looks like a miracle here. Twenty minutes of prompting, marks done, sleep saved. The miracle is real *and* it is also where most teachers get into trouble. The reason isn't that AI grades badly. It's that AI grades *one part* of the essay well and *another part* terribly, and shipping its output unread is the move that damages your classroom for a year.

This lesson gives you the discipline to use AI for the part it's good at, while keeping marks-of-record under your hand. The goal isn't to grade everything yourself. The goal is to grade the things only you can grade, and to outsource the rest *with eyes open*.

blocks.title: Mental model: rubrics are AI's superpower; meaning is yours
blocks.md:
AI is genuinely brilliant at one thing: applying a checklist to text. Give it a 6-criterion rubric and it will tell you, in 12 seconds, which boxes a piece of writing ticks. That's not a bug; that's a feature, and it is the *only* feature you should rely on.

The trouble starts when you ask AI to evaluate the *meaning* of an essay — whether the argument is true, whether the example is well-chosen, whether the writer believes what they wrote. AI will fluently answer all of these. It will be wrong about a quarter of the time, and it cannot tell you when it is wrong.

Use AI for rubric-shaped grading. Keep meaning-shaped grading on your desk.

hi-IN.title: Apni mummy ka quality control
hi-IN.md:
Mummy ko khaana check karne ke do mode hain. Mode 1: "masala daal hai? namak theek hai? thanda toh nahi hua?" — ye AI ka mode hai. Checklist. 4 seconds mein.

Mode 2: "yaar tu thaki hui hai aaj, kya hua?" — ye sirf mummy ka mode hai. Roti ke side se baat *baccha* dikha gaya, jo recipe nahi batati.

AI = Mummy ka Mode 1. Mode 2 ke liye tu hi chahiye, AI nahi.

en.title: Same point, no Hinglish
en.md: There are two kinds of quality check. The checklist kind ("is the salt right? is it cold?") and the relational kind ("why are you tired today?"). AI does the first one fast and well. The second one was never on its menu.

blocks.text: Move 1 — AI-drafted feedback you actually review

blocks.md:
Here is the move that saves you four hours a weekend without costing your classroom anything: **AI drafts the feedback. You review every line before it goes out.**

The trick is in the verbs. AI doesn't *write* feedback that gets sent. AI *drafts* feedback that you then review, edit, and sign off on. Two minutes of review per student replaces twelve minutes of writing per student. Six-x speedup, zero loss of quality, because you're still the last set of eyes.

The failure mode is what teachers call "copy-paste comments." Three students this term tell their parents "ma'am's feedback feels like the same five sentences for everyone." That's not because AI was used. It's because AI was used *and not reviewed*. The review is non-negotiable. If you skip it, you lose the relationship signal that feedback is supposed to carry.

blocks.title: Translation: from 30 essays to 30 reviewed comment sets, on a Sunday, in 70 minutes

steps.label: Step 1 — Write the rubric, then write it again
steps.body: Six criteria. Three or four levels each. The rubric is what AI scores against. If your rubric is fuzzy, every comment will be fuzzy. 10 minutes spent here saves 50 later.

steps.label: Step 2 — Paste 5 essays at a time with the rubric
steps.body: AI returns scored comments per essay. Don't dump all 30 at once; chunk to keep AI's context honest. 5 chunks of 6 essays.

steps.label: Step 3 — Read the AI's comments before reading the essay
steps.body: Counter-intuitive but it works. AI's comment frames your reading. You spot disagreements faster than you spot agreements.

steps.label: Step 4 — Read the essay; flag where AI got it wrong
steps.body: About 1 in 4 essays will have a meaning-level miss. AI praised an argument that doesn't hold up; AI penalised a sentence that was actually clever. These are *yours* to override.

steps.label: Step 5 — Add one personal line per student
steps.body: "Your second paragraph reminded me of the way you argued about the canteen rule last term — you're getting better at this." One line. AI cannot write this. The line is the relationship.

steps.label: Step 6 — Send
steps.body: 70 minutes total. The 12-minutes-per-student version was 6 hours. You bought back a Sunday afternoon without losing the relationship signal.

blocks.prompt: Which use of AI for grading 30 essays is most defensible?

choices.label: Paste essays one by one, accept AI marks, post them
choices.explain: Posting AI marks unread is the entire trap of this lesson. Marks of record are yours.

choices.label: Use AI to score essays against your rubric, read each AI comment, edit ones you disagree with, add a personal line per student, then post
choices.explain: The disciplined version. AI does the structural triage; you keep the meaning check and the personal line.

choices.label: Don't use AI at all; mark every essay manually from scratch
choices.explain: Defensible but expensive. AI's structural pass is useful and cheap; refusing it is leaving free help on the table.

choices.label: Use AI to generate one set of comments and copy-paste it across all 30 students
choices.explain: This is the 'copy-paste comments' failure mode. Students notice; parents notice. Trust takes weeks to rebuild.

hi-IN.title: Riya ka parent meeting
hi-IN.md:
Riya ki mummy report card lekar aayi. "Ma'am, yeh comment toh exact same hai jo Aanya ki report mein hai. Bachchon ne compare kiya WhatsApp pe."

Dono comments AI se generate hue the. Tu review karna bhool gayi thi. Ab Riya ki mummy ke saamne explain karna mushkil — *wo galat nahi hai*. Comments same the.

Moral: copy-paste pakda jata hai. Bachche compare karte hain. Mummies pakad leti hain. AI ka draft hi tha; tujhe review karna tha. Skip nahi kar sakta.

en.title: The parent meeting
en.md: A parent walks in with two report cards open on her phone. The comments are word-for-word identical. The students compared them. The parents found out. AI drafted both; the teacher skipped review. The parent isn't wrong, and the trust takes a term to rebuild.

blocks.md:
Here is a small rule that solves 80% of teacher-AI grading anxiety: **AI is for formative assessment; you do summative.**

Formative = work in progress. Practice essays, draft worksheets, weekly quizzes that won't appear on the final mark. Mistakes here are *good*; the whole point is to learn. AI feedback on formative work, even if it's wrong 10% of the time, is fine. The student catches errors and learns; you save hours; the marks don't go on the record.

Summative = marks of record. Term exams, board prelims, capstone projects. Marks live on a transcript and follow the child for years. AI cannot grade these as the final grader. Use it as a triage tool — reading order, structural pass — and *you* mark.

The distinction is not a guideline; it's a discipline. The day you blur it, you ship marks you can't defend.

coach.name: Principal Priya
coach.role: Your principal, sketching scenarios on a whiteboard between back-to-back meetings

intro: Priya: "Six grading scenarios from last week. Tell me — is this OK to use AI here, or are we asking for trouble?"

scenarios.situation: Your Class 7 students wrote a practice paragraph on their favourite festival. You want quick feedback to send back tomorrow.
scenarios.explain: Formative, low-stakes, structural feedback. AI drafts; you spot-check; it goes back. Exactly what AI exists for.

scenarios.situation: Class 12 board prelim essays. Marks count toward the predicted grades sent to admissions.
scenarios.explain: Summative, high stakes. AI as triage is OK; AI as grader of record is a year-of-the-student decision. You mark.

scenarios.situation: An AI tool writes a personalised parent-meeting summary for each Class 8 student. You glance at the first three and they look fine.
scenarios.explain: "Glance at the first three" is not review. The fourth one might be perfectly polite and factually wrong. Sample bias in your favour, classroom risk against you.

scenarios.situation: Drafting model answers for a Class 10 sample paper to share with the section before the prelim.
scenarios.explain: Formative scaffolding. AI drafts answers; you review for correctness (this is non-trivial!); students get a study aid. Your review fixes the wrong-answer trap.

scenarios.situation: AI detects 'similar phrasing' between two Class 11 essays and tells you it's plagiarism. You're about to mark zero on both.
scenarios.explain: Detector ≠ verdict. "Similar phrasing" is a probabilistic signal. A 5-minute conversation with each student is the actual investigation. Mark zero only after that.

scenarios.situation: Generating six exit-ticket multiple-choice questions on Class 9 Algebra to use in tomorrow's last 10 minutes of class.
scenarios.explain: Formative, AI-friendly, structural work. Just check the keys before printing — AI sometimes mislabels the correct option.

blocks.caption: Watch the trap happen live — and the fix at the end.

blocks.title: The classic trap: AI feedback shipped without reading it
blocks.md:
Sunday night. 30 essays. AI generates feedback in 4 minutes. You hit send.

Monday morning, three things happen. (1) A student notices her comment is identical to her friend's. (2) A parent emails asking why "thrilled by your insightful contribution" appears in their daughter's report when their daughter clearly has not been thrilling anyone. (3) You realise AI praised the *argument* in essay #14, which was actually wrong, and you marked it accordingly.

The fix is mechanical. **You don't ship feedback you haven't read.** Two minutes of review per student. Non-negotiable. If you don't have time to review, you don't have time to grade with AI; the discipline isn't optional.

blocks.prompt: Order these steps the way a disciplined teacher uses AI to grade a stack of formative essays.

items.label: Write or refine your rubric (6 criteria, 3-4 levels)
items.detail: AI scores against this. Fuzzy rubric = fuzzy comments.

items.label: Paste essays in chunks of 5-6 with the rubric
items.detail: Don't overload the AI's context. Chunked input keeps quality up.

items.label: Read AI's comment before reading each essay
items.detail: Counter-intuitive but works. AI's frame surfaces disagreements faster.

items.label: Read essay; flag any meaning-level mistake AI made
items.detail: About 1 in 4 essays will have one. Override. This is your job.

items.label: Add one personal line tied to *this* student's history
items.detail: Cannot be AI-generated. The line carries the relationship.

items.label: Post marks
items.detail: After review, not before.

blocks.hint: Rubric, chunked, AI-comment first, your meaning override, personal line, then send.

blocks.instruction: Take a recent essay prompt you actually used. Write a 6-criterion rubric for it that AI could score against. Each criterion needs 3 levels (e.g. strong / partial / missing).
blocks.starter:
Essay prompt:

Rubric:
1. Criterion: 
   - Strong: 
   - Partial: 
   - Missing: 
2. Criterion: 
   - Strong: 
   - Partial: 
   - Missing: 
3. ... (continue to 6)
blocks.expected:
Essay prompt: Write 400-500 words on whether the Indian Constitution's promise of equality has been delivered for women in your lifetime. Use at least one specific example.

Rubric:
1. Criterion: Thesis clarity
   - Strong: One-sentence thesis stated by paragraph 2; takes a defensible side
   - Partial: Thesis present but hedged or buried
   - Missing: No clear position taken
2. Criterion: Use of specific example
   - Strong: At least one named example with a date or place; example actually supports the thesis
   - Partial: Example named but underdeveloped or weakly tied to thesis
   - Missing: No specific example, only general claims
3. Criterion: Structure (intro / 2-3 body / conclusion)
   - Strong: Clear architecture; each paragraph has one job
   - Partial: Architecture present but one paragraph wanders
   - Missing: No clear paragraph structure
4. Criterion: Counter-argument acknowledgement
   - Strong: Names one objection and addresses it
   - Partial: Names an objection but doesn't address it
   - Missing: No counter-argument
5. Criterion: Language and grammar
   - Strong: Clean prose; under 3 errors per page
   - Partial: Frequent errors but meaning preserved
   - Missing: Errors interfere with meaning
6. Criterion: Voice and originality
   - Strong: Sounds like a Class 11 student who has thought about this; not generic
   - Partial: Some moments of voice, mostly textbook-flavoured
   - Missing: Reads as ChatGPT or copied from a sample paper

blocks.prompt: Pick the practices that keep your AI-assisted grading defensible.

choices.label: Always have your own rubric before opening AI
choices.explain: Yes. Without a rubric, AI grades against its own assumptions, which are generic. With one, you control the criteria.

choices.label: Add one personal line per student before posting
choices.explain: Yes. The personal line is the relationship signal. AI cannot generate it; it's what tells the child that you read their work.

choices.label: Trust AI marks if the AI gives high confidence scores
choices.explain: AI 'confidence' is not the same as accuracy. AI is fluently confident even when wrong; the confidence number is not a safety net.

choices.label: Use AI for marks-of-record on board prelims if you're short on time
choices.explain: This is the line you don't cross. Summative is yours. Short-on-time is a planning problem, not an AI problem.

hi-IN.title: JEE practice set, real life
hi-IN.md:
Tu Class 11 Physics padhata hai, JEE prep wala batch. Har Sunday 50 problems ki practice set ChatGPT se banwata hai — *formative*. Bachchon ko Monday subah milti hai, Wednesday tak khol kar nikaal lete hain. Sab khush.

Lekin term exam? *Summative*. Wahaan tu khud paper banata hai, khud check karta hai. JEE-Main ka asli paper *bachche ki transcript pe jaata hai*; tu AI ko wahaan beech mein nahi laata.

Line simple hai. Practice set = AI se. Marks-of-record = teri kalam se.

en.title: JEE prep, real life
en.md: Weekly practice sets are formative — AI drafts them, students do them, you spot-check. Term exams are summative — they go on a transcript that follows the student to admissions. The line is hard. Practice = AI. Record = your hand.

blocks.title: Field Notes: 30 essays of unread feedback
blocks.source: Anonymous English teacher at a Bangalore international school
blocks.story:
I had 30 personal-narrative essays to grade in 4 days. I gave each one to AI with my rubric (5 criteria × 4 levels) and asked for individualized comments. AI churned out 30 sets of comments in 14 minutes. They looked great. I shipped them.

Day 3: Vihaan's parents emailed. The feedback contradicted itself — paragraph 2 said *"strong opening"*, paragraph 4 said *"weak opening"*. AI hallucinated mid-batch on a tired prompt. **3 of the 30 had the same issue when I checked.** I had to reissue feedback to those 3 students with an apology email cc'd to parents.

The ₹38,000/year ChatGPT Teams subscription paid for itself ten times over in time saved. It also nearly cost me my reputation in 14 minutes of unread output.
blocks.takeaway: AI handles 80%; the 30-second teacher review per essay is what protects the 80% from being a 100% trust problem.

blocks.title: Boss Battle: 32 essays tonight
blocks.setup: It's Tuesday 9 PM. Ms. Anjali has 32 personal-narrative essays from her Class 9 students. Parent-teacher conferences are Saturday. She's tired. She's tempted to ship AI feedback unread.

coach.name: Mentor-Master Mukherjee
coach.role: Retired English HOD, 38 years in Pune schools

stages.prompt: Anjali's first instinct: load the rubric, run all 32 through AI, send. What do you tell her?

options.label: Yes — ship as drafted; she can correct any complaints later.
options.explain: Cover-the-tracks instinct. By the time complaints come, trust is already damaged.

options.label: AI generates 32 drafts; she spends 90 seconds per essay reviewing tone + checking for contradictions before sending.
options.explain: Right balance. ~50 minutes added to a job that was 8 hours; trust preserved.

options.label: Drop the AI; hand-write all 32 from scratch.
options.explain: Burnout-instinct. Wastes the AI's 80% leverage and Anjali still won't have time for the 20% that matters most.

options.label: Send AI drafts but mark them as 'AI-generated, may contain errors'.
options.explain: Feels honest, is actually worse — students and parents now don't trust either the AI's signal or Anjali's editorial judgment.

stages.prompt: On essay #14, Anjali notices the AI praised the 'strong evidence' even though the essay had only one quote (rubric requires 3+). What's the move?

options.label: Override that comment; flag the rest of the AI feedback for closer scrutiny.
options.explain: AI lost calibration mid-batch. The right response is to inspect the rest of THIS batch, not just essay 14.

options.label: Send essay 14 with the wrong comment; she's tired.
options.explain: This is the moment that becomes the parent email Friday morning.

options.label: Re-prompt the AI for essay 14; trust the rest.
options.explain: Calibration loss usually affects multiple essays. Inspect the batch, not just one.

stages.prompt: Saturday at PTM, a parent says 'the AI feedback was great — better than your handwritten notes last term.' How does Anjali respond?

options.label: 'Thank you — I used AI to draft, then reviewed every essay personally before sending.'
options.explain: Honest disclosure + clear ownership. Trust-building.

options.label: 'Thank you — I worked very hard on these.'
options.explain: Half-truth. Will compound badly when AI tools become normalized in schools and disclosure becomes the standard.

options.label: 'I can't really discuss the methodology.'
options.explain: Deflection invites suspicion. Honest is easier.

outcomes.perfect: Clean run. Anjali ships 32 reliable feedback packets in 4 hours instead of 8, parents trust the output, and disclosure becomes a teaching habit. The ₹38K subscription pays for itself in week 1.
outcomes.good: Solid. The discipline holds for 32 essays; one or two close calls but no parent emails. Worth re-running in a month with the same setup.
outcomes.learn: Worth a re-read. The trap here is the 'I'm tired, I'll ship it' moment at essay #20. The 30-second review IS the system.

points: Rubrics are AI's superpower; meaning is yours. Use AI for the structural pass, never for the meaning verdict.
AI drafts feedback; you review every line before it goes out. Two minutes per student replaces twelve.
The personal line per student carries the relationship. AI cannot write it. It is the difference between feedback and noise.
Formative vs summative is a hard line. AI is fine on practice work; marks-of-record stay under your hand.
If you don't have time to review AI feedback, you don't have time to use AI. The discipline is the value.

blocks.prompt: Which student in your class would feel most cheated by copy-paste feedback? Write the personal line you would add to *their* next report. Now you know what AI cannot replace.

lessons.title: AI Detection vs AI Literacy
lessons.subtitle: Stop policing the output; start designing the process

audioChapters.label: Mental model: detection vs honesty design

blocks.md:
Every staff room in India is currently arguing the same fight. "We need a better AI detector." "Ban phones in homework." "Make them write in class." These are downstream symptoms of one upstream design failure: the assignment, as written, can be done by AI in 90 seconds.

Detection is an arms race you cannot win. Models update faster than tools to detect them. Worse, detectors have a real false-positive rate, and the false positives are concentrated on your *strongest* writers — the ones who write in clean, formal English. So the day you mark Riya zero on her board essay because the detector said "92% AI," you may be ending a career on a probability.

This lesson takes a side. You don't win this with detection. You win it with assignments that *require* the process AI can't do, and with a single conversation move that resolves 90% of suspicions in five minutes.

blocks.title: Mental model: don't fight the output, design the process
blocks.md:
When you write an assignment, you implicitly assume something about *how* a student will produce the answer. The traditional essay assumes 5 hours of solitary thinking. AI breaks that assumption; the answer can now be produced in 90 seconds with no thinking at all.

Detection tries to *retroactively* tell whether thinking happened. This is hard, and the tools are weak. **Honesty design** does the opposite: it builds an assignment that *cannot be completed* without the thinking happening. AI can't fake a draft history; it can't fake an oral defence; it can't have been in your second-period last Thursday.

Move the load-bearing wall from the final document to the visible process. The cheating problem largely solves itself.

hi-IN.title: Pakdo-pakdo wala loop
hi-IN.md:
School staff room: "new detector aaya hai, ye pakdega." Doosre hafte: "new detector ne Riya ko galat pakda, parents aa gaye." Teesre hafte: "chalo aur naya detector le lo."

Bhai yeh tom-and-jerry hai. Tu Tom hai, AI Jerry hai, aur Jerry naya cartoon studio open kar raha hai har hafte.

Game badal. Jerry ko maat de, maze ke set se mat khelo — set hi badal de. Process maango, draft maango, viva maango. Jerry ke paas process nahi hota.

en.title: Same point, no Hinglish
en.md: Staff rooms across the country are running the same Tom-and-Jerry routine. Buy detector, students upgrade their tools, false positives explode, repeat. The way out isn't a faster Tom; it's a different game. Make process visible. AI doesn't have one.

blocks.md:
The first move is structural: rewrite the assignment so the *only* way to submit is to produce process artefacts. AI cannot produce these. A student using AI can still cheat, but they have to work hard to fake the process — at which point they're learning anyway, which is the actual goal.

Four patterns to use, alone or stacked:

**Drafts over time.** Submit a draft on Monday, peer-feedback on Wednesday, revision on Friday. The Monday draft can be wrong; what matters is that it's *a* draft. AI doesn't iterate on its own work; the trail of edits is uniquely human.

**Local context anchor.** Use a class-specific prompt that AI doesn't know: "In Tuesday's discussion, Aanya argued X. Take her side and extend the argument." AI was not in your room.

**In-class write.** Last paragraph or full piece, written in the room, no devices. 30 minutes, blue book, your eyes on the desks. The boring kind of test, but it works.

**Annotated bibliography of process.** Ask for a 100-word note on "how I wrote this — what I tried first, what I changed, what I cut." Genuine students write this in three minutes; AI users either skip it (caught) or generate a fake one (also caught — it has the wrong texture).

blocks.title: Translation: rewriting one assignment from AI-shortcutable to honesty-designed

steps.label: Step 1 — The vulnerable original
steps.body: "Class 11 English: write a 600-word essay on whether technology has improved education in India. Submit Friday." 90-second AI job. Zero learning.

steps.label: Step 2 — Add a local context anchor
steps.body: "Begin with last week's class debate where Karan argued the opposite of what most of the class thought. Take Karan's side or rebut it; either way, name his actual argument." AI doesn't know what Karan said.

steps.label: Step 3 — Add a draft requirement
steps.body: "Submit a 200-word draft Monday with one paragraph and three rough notes for the others. Submit revised full draft Friday." Two artefacts. One missing = points off.

steps.label: Step 4 — Add the process bibliography
steps.body: "Append a 100-word note: 'what I tried first, what I changed, what I cut.' Honest answers welcome — saying 'I tried two terrible openings' is fine; saying 'I asked ChatGPT' is also fine if you say *what you did with* what it gave you." The note is itself the assessment of process.

steps.label: Step 5 — Reserve a 5-minute oral check on Friday
steps.body: "Random sample of 5 students will explain one of their paragraphs to me on submission day. Be ready to talk for 90 seconds." Just the *threat* of this changes behaviour.

steps.label: Step 6 — Mark with the new rubric
steps.body: Marks for: process artefacts present, local context engaged, voice consistent across drafts, oral defence credible. The final document is one of five things you grade, not the only thing.

blocks.prompt: Which assignment is *structurally* hardest to AI-shortcut?

choices.label: A 500-word at-home essay on the French Revolution due Friday
choices.explain: Easiest possible target. AI does this in 90 seconds. The final document tells you nothing about whether the student thought.

choices.label: A 500-word essay on the French Revolution, with a Monday draft, a process note, and a 90-second oral check from a 1-in-5 sample
choices.explain: Stacked: process artefacts + sampling + oral check. AI can fake any one of these poorly; faking all three takes longer than just learning the material.

choices.label: A multiple-choice quiz on the French Revolution to be done on the school portal
choices.explain: MCQ at home with phone access is an honour system. AI / Google handles MCQs trivially.

choices.label: A 500-word essay where you'll run it through three different AI detectors after submission
choices.explain: Detection arms race. Detectors share failure modes; running three doesn't fix the false-positive problem and won't catch a careful AI user.

hi-IN.title: Riya wala mamla — false positive
hi-IN.md:
Riya, board-topper category, English mein crisp formal style. AI detector ne 92% "AI-written" bola. Teacher ne zero diya. Riya ke parents principal ke paas. Principal ne paper read kara — clearly Riya hi likhi hai, formal English ki vajah se detector confuse hua.

Teacher: embarrassed.
Riya: betrayed.
Principal: "agli baar conversation pehle, marks zero baad mein."

Detector galat tha. Aur sirf ek baar galat hone se bhi career ka score affect ho gaya. False positive rate is real, aur woh accha bachchon ko sabse zyaada maarta hai.

en.title: The false positive that hurt the strongest student
en.md: Detectors flag formal, polished writing as AI more often than messy writing. Which means your strongest students take the biggest hit. A 92% confidence score is not a verdict; it is a hint. Always have the conversation before marking the zero.

blocks.md:
The single most powerful tool in your honesty toolkit takes 5 minutes per student and costs nothing: **the oral defence.**

Mechanic: pick a paragraph from the student's submission. Ask them to explain *why they made one specific edit, why they chose that example, what they considered and rejected*. A student who wrote the essay can answer this in 30 seconds, even badly. A student who pasted from AI freezes — not because they're stupid, but because the editing decisions never happened in their head.

It does not matter if the AI is sophisticated. The oral defence isn't testing the writing; it's testing whether the writer's mind owns the writing. There is no current AI workflow that produces this signal.

Use it as policy: *every essay above grade X is subject to a 5% random oral check on submission day. If your essay is selected and you cannot explain a paragraph, marks are reduced.* The 5% is enough; you don't need to interview everyone. The threat alone changes behaviour.
