coach.role: Your principal, holding a stack of detector reports and a coffee

intro: Priya: "Six suspicions from this week. Tell me — proceed with consequences, or have a conversation first?"

scenarios.situation: Aanya submitted a debate speech that's structurally polished and oddly hollow. Detector says 78%. She's a B-grade English student normally.
scenarios.explain: Suggestive, not conclusive. A 90-second oral extension on the topic tomorrow tells you everything. Detector is one signal; conversation is the verdict.

scenarios.situation: Karan and Mehul submitted essays where the central paragraph is word-for-word identical, and both contain an Indian historical fact that's *factually wrong*.
scenarios.explain: Identical paragraph + matching factual error is the actual smoking gun. Same source, near-certainly. You can still ask, but the consequences are warranted.

scenarios.situation: Riya, a top student, gets flagged 92% AI by your detector. Her writing has always been polished and formal.
scenarios.explain: Classic false-positive zone. Polished formal writers trigger detectors. Five-minute oral on her draft choices and you'll know in 90 seconds.

scenarios.situation: Aarav cheerfully tells you he 'used ChatGPT to fix the grammar' on his English assignment.
scenarios.explain: Self-disclosure is a teaching moment. Ask to see the rough draft *before* the polish; grade the gap. He may have done more work than he thinks.

scenarios.situation: An entire batch of 4 essays has the same opening sentence about 'in today's rapidly evolving world'. Detector flags all 4.
scenarios.explain: Common AI tell, repeated across 4 students. Conversation can still happen, but a class-wide reset on the rubric is warranted; this isn't a one-student situation.

scenarios.situation: Mira's essay sounds nothing like her in-class voice. No detector flag, but your gut says something is off.
scenarios.explain: Your gut is calibrated by 20+ essays of Mira's. That signal is more reliable than a detector. Conversation, not consequences. Your gut deserves a 5-minute check.

blocks.caption: Watch the trap happen live — and the fix at the end.

blocks.title: The classic trap: false positives ruin a good student
blocks.md:
The detector said 92%. You marked the zero. The student's parents come in. The student is your strongest English writer; her writing has always been formal and clean.

You now have a problem. The detector was wrong. The marks-of-record have a zero on them. The student's relationship with English class is now poisoned for the rest of the year. Your reputation in the staff room is one explanation away from "the one who marked Riya zero on a probability score."

**Rule:** detectors are hints, never verdicts. Always have the 5-minute conversation before any consequence touches the student's record. If you skip the conversation, you are accepting that some good students will pay for the false-positive rate of a tool you didn't build.

blocks.prompt: Order these steps the way a fair teacher handles a suspected AI submission.

items.label: Note the suspicion privately; don't mark anything yet
items.detail: Do nothing irreversible while the only evidence is a probabilistic signal.

items.label: Re-read the submission yourself
items.detail: Does *your* gut agree with the detector? Your gut has more context than the tool.

items.label: Ask the student a 5-minute oral about their drafting choices
items.detail: Specific paragraph, specific edit. Why this word, why this example.

items.label: Listen for ownership signal: hesitation is fine; total absence of edit history is the tell
items.detail: Real writers know what they cut. AI users don't, because they didn't cut anything.

items.label: If unresolved, ask for the rough draft and one extension paragraph in class tomorrow
items.detail: Two more low-stakes data points before any consequence.

items.label: Apply consequences only after multiple converging signals, never on one detector score
items.detail: And document the conversation, not the score, as the basis.

blocks.hint: Never mark consequences on a probability score. Conversation is fast; reputation damage is permanent.

blocks.instruction: Take an assignment you currently use that an AI could complete in 90 seconds. Rewrite it as an honesty-designed version stacking 2-3 of the four moves (drafts, local anchor, in-class write, process bibliography).
blocks.starter:
Original assignment (vulnerable):

Rewritten assignment (honesty-designed):
- Local context anchor:
- Draft / process artefact:
- In-class component (if any):
- Process note / oral check:
- New rubric (briefly):
blocks.expected:
Original assignment (vulnerable): "Class 10 English: Write a 600-word essay on whether social media is a net positive or negative for Indian teenagers. Submit Friday."

Rewritten assignment (honesty-designed):
- Local context anchor: "Begin by referencing the WhatsApp group rumour that spread through 9-B last week (the 'cricket coach' story). Use it as a case in point or a counter-example, but you must engage with what actually happened."
- Draft / process artefact: "Submit a 150-word draft Tuesday with thesis + one example. Final 600 words Friday. Both required; missing draft = -10%."
- In-class component: "Friday's last paragraph (60-80 words) written in class, no devices, on lined paper, 15 minutes. This becomes the closing of your essay."
- Process note: "Append 80 words: what I tried first, what I changed, what I cut. Honest answers welcome."
- Oral check: "5% random sample on submission day will be asked to explain one of their paragraph edits in 90 seconds."
- New rubric: 30% argument quality | 20% local-context engagement | 20% process artefacts present | 20% in-class paragraph quality | 10% process note specificity

blocks.prompt: Which combinations of honesty-design moves produce structurally robust assignments? (Pick the strong ones.)

choices.label: Drafts over time + 5% oral defence sampling
choices.explain: Yes. Two cheap, low-friction layers that AI shortcutting can't fake at scale.

choices.label: Local context anchor + process bibliography
choices.explain: Yes. The anchor blocks generic AI output; the bibliography asks the student to narrate the work, which AI users find awkward.

choices.label: Three different AI detectors run on every submission
choices.explain: Detection arms race. Detectors share failure modes; running three doesn't fix the structural problem and amplifies false positives.

choices.label: Banning AI entirely and threatening expulsion
choices.explain: Bans push behaviour underground; you lose the signal you'd otherwise see. Discipline is downstream of design.

hi-IN.title: VIVA culture, repurposed
hi-IN.md:
India mein VIVA ka culture purana hai. Class 10 Maths VIVA, Class 12 Practical VIVA — bachche tayar hote the. ChatGPT ne essay culture todi, lekin VIVA culture ko revive kiya hai, in a way.

5 minute ka oral defence — yeh exactly woh skill hai jo VIVA mein kaam aati thi. Bachcha apni hi paper explain kar sake. Wapis se relevant ho gayi.

Matlab AI ne pedagogy ko 1990 ke pre-PowerPoint era mein wapis ek step bheja hai — aur it's *not* a bad thing.

en.title: The viva is back
en.md: Indian schools have a long tradition of vivas — students explaining their own answers in person. AI has accidentally made vivas relevant again. The skill of explaining your own paragraph is exactly the skill the AI shortcut bypasses.

blocks.title: Field Notes: a debate-club kid flagged as AI
blocks.source: Anonymous English teacher at a Delhi CBSE school
blocks.story:
Aarush is in Class 12. State-level debate champion. Speaks in fully-formed paragraphs. Writes in fully-formed paragraphs. Three different AI detectors flagged his Term 2 essay as 88-94% AI-written.

I confronted him. He cried. His mother accused me of bias. Principal got involved. We finally agreed on a rerun: Aarush wrote the next essay in class with a stopwatch and process notes. Result: indistinguishable from his Term 2 work.

The detector was 'right' in the statistical sense — Aarush's writing matches AI-trained patterns. The detector was *catastrophically wrong* in the case-level sense. I wrote the school an apology that week. **I now design assignments that don't require detection at all** — in-class drafts, oral defenses, process journals.
blocks.takeaway: Detector arms races punish your structured-prose students; honesty-design beats detection every time.

blocks.title: Boss Battle: 5 essays flagged
blocks.setup: Ms. Anjali's AI detector (free Chrome extension, 'works pretty well') flags 5 of her 32 Class 11 history essays as AI-written. One is from her top student (debate club, native English speaker). One is from a student who has never used the school computers. The remaining 3 are first-year students new to academic writing.

coach.name: Dean-of-Teaching Devika
coach.role: Heads pedagogy at a CBSE school chain across 14 cities

stages.prompt: First instinct: confront all 5 students based on detector output. What does Devika say?

options.label: Yes — investigate all 5 immediately, give them zeros if they can't explain.
options.explain: Detector false-positive rate is ~15-25% on structured-prose writers. Confronting all 5 will burn your top student's trust within an hour.

options.label: Pause. Detector is a signal, not evidence. Look at writing history for each student first.
options.explain: Right move. Detector is one input among many. Compare to historical writing samples, draft history, in-class work.

options.label: Trust the detector — false positives are statistically rare.
options.explain: False. False-positive rate on structured-prose writers can hit 25%+. Statistical rare ≠ case-level rare for this cohort.

options.label: Ignore the detector entirely. AI is fine.
options.explain: Overcorrection. Detector signal still matters; it's just not evidence on its own.

stages.prompt: After review: 2 essays show clear AI usage (no draft history, generic structure, factual errors). 3 essays match the students' historical writing (including the debate club kid). What's the move?

options.label: Confront the 2 with evidence; have a conversation with the 3 about the false-positive risk and how she'll redesign assignments.
options.explain: Right balance. Action where the evidence is solid; transparency where the signal was false.

options.label: Treat all 5 the same — 'fairness'.
options.explain: Equal treatment of unequal evidence is unfair. The 3 students didn't do anything wrong; treating them as if they did damages trust.

options.label: Give all 5 a redo with 'no AI allowed'.
options.explain: Punishes the 3 innocent students; doesn't change the 2 actual AI users' incentives unless redo is supervised.

stages.prompt: Looking forward: Anjali wants to prevent this whole cycle next term. What's the structural fix?

options.label: Buy a better AI detector; pay for the premium tier.
options.explain: Detector arms race. The kids will use better AI; you'll pay more for marginally better detection. Lose-lose.

options.label: Redesign assignments to require process — in-class drafting, oral defense, mid-draft check-ins.
options.explain: Honesty-design. AI can produce polished output; it cannot fake a 30-min in-class draft + an oral defense.

options.label: Ban AI school-wide and threaten suspension.
options.explain: Unenforceable. Drives the problem underground; trust drops; smart kids find better cover.

options.label: Make peace with the detector noise.
options.explain: Detector arms race continues; you keep losing your structured-prose students every term.

outcomes.perfect: S-tier. Anjali avoids the trust catastrophe with her debate-club kid AND redesigns the next term's assignments around process. The detector becomes one signal among five, never the verdict.
outcomes.good: Solid handling. The 2 actual AI cases get caught; the 3 false positives don't get burned. Worth running the redesign next term.
outcomes.learn: Re-read the false-positive section. The detector's statistical accuracy says nothing about the case in front of you.

points: Detection is an arms race you cannot win; honesty design is one-time work that holds.
Stack two or more moves — drafts over time, local anchor, in-class write, process bibliography. Two layers is enough.
The 5-minute oral defence resolves 90% of suspicions. It tests ownership of edits, which AI cannot fake.
Detector scores are hints, never verdicts. Always have the conversation before the consequence touches a student's record.
False positives concentrate on your strongest writers. Marking zero on a probability score is how you damage a top student's year.

blocks.prompt: Which student would suffer most if your AI detector hit a false positive on them? What conversation would you want to have *before* any consequences? Now write that conversation into your assignment policy.

lessons.title: Run a 14-Day Classroom Experiment
lessons.subtitle: A baseline, three numbers, and a kill criterion

blocks.md:
Most of what passes for "AI works in my classroom" is vibes. A teacher tries a tool for two weeks, students seem more engaged, the teacher reports it as a win. Two months later the tool is forgotten, the worksheets are back to xerox, and nobody can say whether anything actually changed.

The problem isn't that the teacher was wrong. The problem is that they didn't run an experiment; they ran a vibe check. A vibe check tells you how *you* feel about the tool. An experiment tells you whether the tool moved the numbers you actually care about.

This lesson hands you a 14-day experiment template that fits inside one term, costs nothing, and gives you a defensible answer at the end. Do this once and you'll never have to argue with the staff room about "AI tools" again — you'll have your own data.

blocks.title: Mental model: a tracked intervention with three numbers
blocks.md:
Think of the experiment as a small, tracked change. You change one thing — the AI tool — and you watch what happens to *three* numbers across two weeks.

Number 1: an outcome you care about. Quiz averages, time-on-task, error rate.
Number 2: a cost you care about. Your prep time, your grading time, the number of late-night Sundays.
Number 3: a relationship signal. "My teacher knows me" on a 1-5 scale; or how many times this fortnight you walked over to a struggling student during class.

Three numbers, two weeks, one decision. The whole apparatus fits on one A4 page. The discipline isn't in the rigour; it's in the *commitment to look at the numbers honestly* on day 14.

blocks.caption: Watch a 14-day experiment unfold across three lines: outcome, cost, relationship. Drag day-14 to see the decision logic.

hi-IN.title: Diet wala analogy
hi-IN.md:
Tu kabhi diet ki hai? Bina baseline weight liye? Bina daily-check kiye? Sirf "hum healthy kha rahe hain" feeling pe?

Bhai, 3 hafte baad tu khud nahi keh sakta kuch hua bhi ki nahi. Diet *to be tracked* hoti hai, varna woh *vibe* hai, intervention nahi.

Classroom AI experiment bhi waisa hi. 14 din pehle weigh karo (baseline), 14 din baad weigh karo (post). Beech mein 3 numbers track karo — outcome, cost, relationship. Bina baseline ke aap khud ko fool kar rahe ho.

en.title: The diet analogy
en.md: Have you ever started a diet without weighing yourself first? Three weeks in, you cannot tell if anything changed. Classroom AI is the same: no baseline, no experiment, just a feeling that something happened.

blocks.md:
The design fits on one page. Three numbers, three captures, one decision rule.

**Pick your three numbers, before day 1.** Not generically; *for this experiment*. If you're testing AI-generated practice problems for Class 10 Maths, your numbers might be: weekly quiz average (outcome), Sunday prep hours (cost), end-of-fortnight "my teacher knows what I'm struggling with" 1-5 scale from anonymous student survey (relationship). Three concrete numbers anchored to *this specific tool, this specific class.*

**Capture each number twice: baseline and post.** Day 0: write down the three current values. Day 14: write down the three new values. The act of writing the baseline before you start is the discipline; without it, you remember the past as whatever supports your current feeling.

**Set a kill criterion.** Before you start, write: "if X drops by Y, I stop." Not "I'll think about it"; a real number that triggers a real decision. Most experiments don't have one and run forever, which is why most aren't experiments.

blocks.title: Translation: 14 days, three numbers, one decision

steps.label: Day 0 — Capture baseline
steps.body: Write down the three current values *before* starting. "Last 4 weeks: quiz avg 68%, Sunday prep 4 hrs, last student survey: 3.8/5." Five minutes.

steps.label: Days 1-7 — Run intervention week 1
steps.body: Use the AI tool consistently as designed. Don't change the design mid-week. Don't combine with other new things — that confounds the experiment.

steps.label: Day 7 — Mid-point gut check (no decisions)
steps.body: Quick note on a sticky: how does it *feel*? Worth re-reading on day 14 to see how the gut compared to the data.

steps.label: Days 8-14 — Run intervention week 2
steps.body: Same tool, same design. Continue capturing the data points (weekly quiz, time logs, day-13 survey).

steps.label: Day 14 — Capture post values
steps.body: Three numbers, written down. "Quiz avg 71%, Sunday prep 2.5 hrs, survey 3.7/5." Don't editorialise — just the numbers.

steps.label: Day 14 — Make the decision
steps.body: Apply your decision rule. Outcome up, cost down, relationship roughly flat → keep. Outcome flat, cost down, relationship dropped → keep but redirect saved time. Any number breached the kill criterion → stop. The rule is the whole point.

blocks.prompt: You're about to start a 14-day pilot of an AI worksheet tool for Class 7 Hindi. Day 0 is tomorrow. The single most important thing to do *today* is:

choices.label: Pick the most exciting AI tool from a free-trial review
choices.explain: Tool selection is necessary but not sufficient. You can pilot the right tool with no baseline and learn nothing.

choices.label: Capture three baseline numbers in writing — outcome, cost, relationship
choices.explain: Yes. No baseline means no experiment. Day 0 is the only day you can take the 'before' picture. Miss it and you cannot recover.

choices.label: Write a long blog post about why AI is the future of education
choices.explain: Marketing the experiment is not running the experiment. The data either supports a claim or doesn't; opinion pieces don't substitute.

choices.label: Tell parents about the experiment for transparency
choices.explain: Communication matters but doesn't change whether the experiment works. Capture the baseline first; communicate this week.

hi-IN.title: Sneha ma'am ka 14-day sting
hi-IN.md:
Sneha ma'am, Pune ki Marathi-medium school. Class 8 ko science worksheet AI se banwane ka decide kiya — 14 din. Day 0 pe likh ke rakha: weekly quiz avg 62%, Sunday prep 5 hrs, student-likeability ek small chit pe 3.4/5.

Day 14: avg 64% (no real change), prep 2 hrs (saved 3!), likeability 3.4 (no change).

Decision: KEEP, kyunki cost gir gaya bina kuch break kiye. *Aur* unho ne saved 3 hrs ko 1-on-1 student check-ins mein redirect kiya. Day 28 likeability check pe — 3.8 ho gaya. Yeh wahi loop hai jo course pura sikha raha hai.

en.title: Sneha's 14-day sting
en.md: A Pune Marathi-medium teacher ran a 14-day pilot. Outcome unchanged, cost dropped 3 hrs, relationship flat. She kept the tool, redirected the saved 3 hrs into 1-on-1 check-ins, and watched the relationship score climb the next fortnight. The boring 80% saved time funded the human 20%.

blocks.md:
Day 14 is the only day that matters. Everything before it is data collection; everything after is execution of the decision. The decision itself takes 10 minutes if you've done the design honestly.

**Apply the rule, don't argue with it.** If you wrote "if relationship drops by more than 0.5, I stop," and relationship dropped by 0.7, you stop. Even if the outcome went up. Even if cost dropped. The rule existed to protect you from your own commitment bias — *especially* to a tool you wanted to like.

**The four-quadrant decision.** Outcome ↑ + cost ↓ → keep, expand. Outcome flat + cost ↓ → keep, redirect saved time. Outcome ↓ + cost ↓ → kill (you saved time at the wrong cost). Outcome ↑ + cost ↑ → think harder; what would you give up to keep this?

**The relationship signal beats both.** If "my teacher knows me" dropped, no amount of outcome and cost wins justifies continuing. The whole point of saving time on the boring 80% was to protect the human 20%; if you trade them, you've inverted the model.

scenarios.situation: Anita ma'am, Class 8 English: quiz avg up from 62% to 71%, prep time down 4hrs to 2hrs, student-knows-me survey 3.6 → 3.7.
scenarios.explain: Outcome up, cost down, relationship steady. Cherish this quadrant — it's rare. Keep, expand to other sections.

scenarios.situation: Rajesh sir, Class 11 Physics: quiz avg unchanged at 64%, prep time down 5hrs to 2.5hrs, relationship 3.9 → 3.8.
scenarios.explain: Cost dropped 50% with no harm. Keep the tool; spend the saved 2.5 hrs on 1-on-1 doubt-clearing, which is the human 20%.

scenarios.situation: Pooja ma'am, Class 10 Maths: quiz avg up from 70% to 76%, prep down 3hrs to 1hr, BUT 'my teacher knows me' dropped 4.0 → 3.0.
scenarios.explain: Relationship signal breached. The 1-point drop on the relationship scale is the override. You saved time at the wrong cost. Kill or redesign before continuing.

scenarios.situation: Mohan sir, Class 9 Civics: quiz avg dropped from 68% to 61%, prep time down 4hrs to 2hrs, relationship steady.
scenarios.explain: Outcome dropped meaningfully (7 points). Even if cost dropped, you traded student learning for your weekend. That's the wrong way around. Kill.

scenarios.situation: Asha ma'am, Class 7 Hindi: quiz avg up 60% to 64%, prep time *increased* 3hrs to 4.5hrs, relationship steady.

blocks.title: The classic trap: shipped without baseline
blocks.md:
You started using the AI tool three weeks ago. Things 'feel better.' You're recommending it in the staff room.

But you didn't write down the baseline. You can't actually compare. Your "things feel better" is what every teacher in every fad's first week has felt. You will, two months from now, not remember whether quiz averages went up, stayed flat, or dropped — because the only data you have is your impression of how it felt, which is exactly the kind of data that gets corrected by hindsight.

**Rule:** if you didn't write the baseline before day 1, you are running a vibe check, not an experiment. Don't recommend it to colleagues. Don't write a blog post. Restart with a baseline next term.

blocks.prompt: Order these steps the way a disciplined teacher runs a 14-day classroom AI experiment.

items.label: Pick three numbers (outcome, cost, relationship) specific to the tool and class
items.detail: Generic numbers ("engagement") don't help; specific ones do.

items.label: Write a kill criterion before day 1
items.detail: "If relationship drops by 0.5 or more, I stop." Real number, real trigger.

items.label: Capture baseline values (day 0)
items.detail: In writing. On paper or a sheet. Not in your head.

items.label: Run the intervention consistently for 14 days, no other new variables
items.detail: Don't try three new tools at once; you can't tell which one moved the numbers.

items.label: Capture post values on day 14
items.detail: Same three numbers. Don't editorialise; just record.

items.label: Apply the four-quadrant decision rule
items.detail: Including the relationship-signal override. Decide and execute.

blocks.prompt: Pick the things that make a 14-day classroom AI experiment *real* (not a vibe check).

choices.label: A baseline number captured in writing before day 1
choices.explain: Yes. The day-0 baseline is the only thing that lets you compare. Without it, day-14 numbers are just numbers.

choices.label: A pre-written kill criterion
choices.explain: Yes. Without one, the experiment runs forever and you protect a tool you wanted to like, even when it's hurting students.

choices.label: Try a different AI tool every 2 days for variety
choices.explain: Confounded variables. You won't know which tool moved which number; you've run 7 experiments at once and can't conclude any.

choices.label: A baseline 'gut feel' that things will work
choices.explain: Gut feel is the thing the experiment is meant to *correct*. Capturing your prior gut feeling isn't the same as capturing data.

hi-IN.title: Staff room mein experimentwallah ban gaya
hi-IN.md:

Is term shuru se baseline kar liya. Day 14 pe ek line bola: "prep time 4 hrs se 2 hrs, quiz avg 65 se 68, relationship 3.7 se 3.8." Pura staff room ne sun liya. Principal ne policy team mein invite kar liya.

Vibes opinion hai. Numbers credibility hai. Bilkul wahi line jo tu bachchon ko sikhata hai for science fair — abhi tu hi follow kar.

en.title: Same point, no Hinglish
en.md: Vibes get you ignored in staff meetings. Numbers get you invited to the policy committee. The credibility difference is just whether you wrote the baseline down on day zero — the smallest possible unit of effort, the largest possible difference in being taken seriously.

blocks.title: Field Notes: 'feels better' isn't a result
blocks.source: Anonymous Class 8 science teacher at a Chennai CBSE school
blocks.story:
I introduced AI-drafted exit tickets in October. By December, principal asked: 'did it work?'

I said *"feels like yes."* She asked: *"compared to what?"*

I hadn't taken a baseline. I hadn't tracked test scores by chapter, prep time, or class engagement. I had a gut feeling and 14 weeks of zero data. **Principal pulled the ₹47,000 budget for next term's tools.**

That experience taught me what 14 days of baseline data would have unlocked. I now run all classroom experiments with three numbers: average chapter test score (before/after), my own prep time per week, and a 1-5 engagement rating I write down on Friday. I've kept this for 8 months. The two interventions that 'felt great' actually showed nothing measurable. The one I almost killed showed +14% on test scores.
blocks.takeaway: 'Feels better' isn't a result — three numbers tracked over 14 days is the cheapest insurance against losing your classroom-AI budget.

blocks.title: Boss Battle: did the experiment work?
blocks.setup: Ms. Anjali ran an AI experiment in her Class 9 history classroom for 14 days: AI-generated practice questions sent home as nightly review. Now her principal asks the question: *did it work?* Anjali has no baseline data. She has a feeling.

coach.name: Mentor-Master Mukherjee
coach.role: Retired English HOD, 38 years in Pune schools

stages.prompt: First instinct: tell the principal *"feels like the kids are more engaged."* What's the issue?

options.label: Nothing — engagement is hard to measure anyway.
options.explain: This is exactly the response that gets the AI tooling budget killed. The principal needs governance evidence, not feelings.

options.label: 'Feels like' is unverifiable; the principal can't justify the budget on a feeling.
options.explain: Right. 'Feels like' is the trap. From now on, design experiments with a baseline before they start.

options.label: Feeling counts more than data when teachers are the ones running the experiment.
options.explain: Teacher intuition matters, but it cannot SUBSTITUTE for measurement when budget is on the line.

stages.prompt: Anjali wants to design the next experiment properly. Which 3 numbers should she track?

options.label: Average chapter test score · weekly prep time · weekly engagement rating (1-5)
options.explain: Three numbers, two minutes a week, captures outcome (test) + cost (prep) + texture (engagement). The right minimum.

options.label: Just test scores; that's the only objective metric.
options.explain: Misses the cost side. If test scores rise but prep time triples, the intervention isn't viable at scale.

options.label: Track 14 different metrics across spreadsheet tabs.
options.explain: Dashboard delusion. Too many metrics = updated twice = abandoned. Three is the cap.

options.label: Just engagement; tests are stress.
options.explain: Engagement alone is fakeable; principals will (correctly) ignore it without an outcome metric.

stages.prompt: Day 14 of the next experiment. Test scores +12%, prep time -8%, engagement 4.2/5 (was 3.6). What's the right read?

options.label: Modify with caution; one chapter's worth of data, but signal is encouraging — run another 14 days.
options.explain: Right. 14 days is enough to keep going; not enough to declare victory. A second 14-day run validates.

options.label: Massive success — apply to all classes immediately.
options.explain: Single 14-day result on one chapter; could be the chapter, not the intervention. Run another cycle before scaling.

options.label: Kill it; numbers can't be trusted on n=1 chapter.
options.explain: Overcorrection. Numbers are encouraging; another cycle is the right next move, not abandonment.

outcomes.perfect: Anjali walks out of the principal's office with the AI budget renewed AND a 14-day experiment template that she'll reuse every term. Three numbers, two minutes a week, irrefutable signal.
outcomes.good: Solid. The principal sees discipline; budget held. Worth a second 14-day cycle to validate.
outcomes.learn: Re-read the baseline section. 'Feels like' is the most expensive sentence in classroom AI.

points: An experiment is a tracked intervention with three numbers — outcome, cost, relationship — captured on day 0 and day 14.
No baseline, no experiment. The 5 minutes you spend writing baseline numbers on day 0 cannot be recovered later.
Pre-write a kill criterion. Without one, you'll protect a tool you wanted to like even when the data says stop.
The relationship signal beats outcome and cost. If 'my teacher knows me' dropped, you stop, regardless of how much time you saved.
Saved time is not the win; the win is what you redirect the saved time toward. The boring 80% buys you the human 20%.

blocks.prompt: What is the *one* AI tool or workflow you'd want to test in your classroom this term? Write your three numbers right now, before reading anything else. If you can't pick three, the experiment isn't ready.

assessment.title: AI for Teachers Assessment
assessment.description: Tests whether you can apply the boring-80/human-20 line to real classroom decisions: prep, assessment, honesty design, and a tracked experiment. The wrong answers are the well-meaning ones; that is the point.

questions.stem: You teach Class 9 Science in a CBSE school. You have 90 minutes before the next class. Which of these is the *least* defensible use of AI?

choices.label: Drafting six exit-ticket questions on chemical reactions
choices.explanation: Boring 80%. AI does this well. You still pick which six to actually use.

choices.label: Writing a summary of yesterday's class for an absent student
choices.explanation: Boring 80%. Cheap, fast, harmless if you skim it.

choices.label: Reading the AI's three-paragraph reply to Aarav's bereavement email and deciding whether to send it as is
choices.explanation: Correct. The AI may produce technically polite words, but the human 20% is reading the room. You don't outsource a condolence; you draft, then write your own.

choices.label: Generating five MCQs from the NCERT chapter on the Periodic Table
choices.explanation: Boring 80% with mandatory review. Fine to draft; you check the keys before printing.

questions.stem: Pick the prompts that are likely to give you a *usable* lesson plan on the first try (not the third).

choices.label: "Write a lesson plan on photosynthesis."
choices.explanation: Generic prompt, generic output. No grade, no time, no outcome. You'll spend 20 minutes editing what 90 seconds of context would have prevented.

choices.label: "You are a Class 7 ICSE Science teacher in a Pune school. 35 mixed-ability students, 40 minute period. By the end, students should be able to label inputs and outputs of photosynthesis on a leaf diagram. Plan it."
choices.explanation: Outcome-first, grade-anchored, time-bounded. AI now has a real brief and produces something close to class-ready.

choices.label: "Make this lesson harder, but do not use the word 'photosynthesis' in the first 3 minutes."
choices.explanation: Iterative refinement after a first draft. Constraint plus revision is where AI earns its keep; you are now directing, not begging.

choices.label: "Be creative."
choices.explanation: Adjective without scaffolding. AI will produce a creative-sounding mush. 'Creative' is your job; structure is its job.

questions.stem: You ran 30 Class 10 essays through an AI feedback tool. The AI marked Anika's essay as the strongest. You haven't read any of them yet. What's the right next step?

choices.label: Trust the AI's ranking and post the marks tonight; you have a parent meeting at 8am
choices.explanation: This is exactly the trap. AI grades structure well and meaning poorly. Anika's essay may be a polished argument that's wrong. Marks posted unread is reputation roulette.

choices.label: Read the top-ranked and bottom-ranked essays first to calibrate, then sample five from the middle
choices.explanation: Correct. Calibrate, then sample. AI's role is to triage your reading order, not replace it. Middle-band sampling catches the cases where structure and meaning diverge.

choices.label: Mark every essay yourself ignoring the AI output to be safe
choices.explanation: Not wrong, but it throws away the cheap signal. The AI's ranking is useful as a reading order even if you don't trust the marks.

choices.label: Ask the AI to mark again with a stricter prompt and trust the second pass
choices.explanation: Two AI passes are still no human read. The fundamental issue is meaning; doubling the structure check doesn't fix it.

questions.stem: Which assignments make AI cheating *structurally* harder, not just punishable?

choices.label: An essay submitted as a final document
choices.explanation: Easiest possible thing for AI to produce. The student's final document tells you nothing about the process behind it.

choices.label: An essay where the student must submit three drafts plus a 5-minute oral defence on chosen edits
choices.explanation: Process-anchored. The defence reveals whether the student actually owns the argument; AI cannot defend an essay it wrote without you noticing.

choices.label: A worksheet that tests recall of yesterday's lecture
choices.explanation: Recall is exactly what AI is best at. Recall worksheets are an AI honor system.

choices.label: A class-specific case study using a local example only your students saw, with a 15-minute in-class write
choices.explanation: Local context plus in-class constraint is the cleanest defence. AI doesn't know what happened in your second period; you do.

questions.stem: Your AI detector flags Riya's essay as 92% AI-written. Riya is your strongest English student. What is the most defensible move?

choices.label: Mark it zero with the detector report attached as evidence
choices.explanation: Detectors have a real false-positive rate, especially on strong, formal writers. A zero based on this is the kind of decision that ends up in the principal's office, with you on the wrong side.

choices.label: Have a 10-minute conversation with Riya about her draft choices: which paragraph she rewrote, why she chose her examples
choices.explanation: Correct. The detector is a hint, not a verdict. A short oral check costs you 10 minutes and tells you what 10 detectors won't.

choices.label: Forward the detector report to her parents and let them handle it
choices.explanation: Outsourcing a judgment call to people with less context, on the strength of a probabilistic score. Bad for Riya, bad for your relationship with the family.

choices.label: Run the essay through three more detectors and average the scores
choices.explanation: Detectors share failure modes. Averaging three fragile signals doesn't produce a robust one.

questions.stem: You want to test whether AI-generated practice problems improve your Class 12 Maths students' JEE prep. You are about to start a 14-day pilot. The most important thing to do *before* day 1 is:

choices.label: Pick an exciting AI tool with a free trial
choices.explanation: The tool isn't the experiment. You can trial five tools and learn nothing if you skipped the next step.

choices.label: Capture a baseline: current weekly test averages and the time you currently spend making practice sets
choices.explanation: Correct. No baseline, no experiment. You are running a vibe check. The whole point of 14 days is comparing two numbers; one of them has to exist before day 1.

choices.label: Tell parents you're doing an AI experiment
choices.explanation: Communication matters, but it doesn't change whether the experiment works. It changes blame allocation, which is not the same thing.

choices.label: Decide whether to keep using AI long-term
choices.explanation: That decision is what the experiment produces. Making it on day 0 means you don't need an experiment.

questions.stem: Which of these signals tell you the boring 80% / human 20% line has been *crossed* in the wrong direction?

choices.label: You haven't read a student essay in two weeks because the AI summary is good enough
choices.explanation: Yes. The summary may be good. Your relationship with the student's actual writing is gone. That's the human 20% leaking out.

choices.label: You used AI to draft 12 questions, picked 5, edited 2
choices.explanation: This is the line working as designed. Draft, select, edit.

choices.label: Three students this week told you their feedback comments felt copy-pasted
choices.explanation: Yes. They can tell. The whole point of feedback is the child knowing you saw their work; AI feedback shipped without your hand on it loses that signal.

choices.label: You tried Claude this morning and made an exit ticket in 90 seconds
choices.explanation: That's the win. 90 seconds saved is 90 seconds you have to walk past Aarav's desk.

questions.stem: Aarav is in Class 8, struggles with English, and tells you he uses ChatGPT to "polish" his homework. The pedagogically defensible response is:

choices.label: Ban ChatGPT and warn him you'll mark zero next time
choices.explanation: Bans push the behaviour underground; you lose the signal he just gave you. A child who tells you what tool he used is a teaching opportunity, not a discipline case.

choices.label: Ask him to show you the version *before* polishing and the version after, and grade the gap
choices.explanation: Correct. You preserved the learning signal (the rough draft is his thinking) and made the AI's role visible. Now you can teach him to write, not police him.

choices.label: Tell him polishing is fine and stop asking
choices.explanation: You handed back a learning event for an easier life. He'll keep submitting polished mush; you'll never see how his sentences actually move.

choices.label: Run his work through an AI detector first and then decide
choices.explanation: He already told you. You don't need a detector. You need a teaching move.

questions.stem: You teach in a Marathi-medium school in Pune. AI tools are mostly trained on English. The best first use of AI in your prep is:

choices.label: Have the AI translate everything to Marathi and use it directly
choices.explanation: AI Marathi is uneven. Direct paste means you'll find idiom-level errors in front of 35 children, on the board.

choices.label: Have the AI draft structure (lesson outline, question stems, rubric) in English; you write the Marathi version
choices.explanation: Correct. Use AI where it's strong (structure, taxonomy of question types). Keep the language layer with you, where the local fluency lives.

choices.label: Avoid AI until it's good in Marathi
choices.explanation: You're leaving the structural help on the table. Lesson outlines, rubric drafts, summary templates work in English just fine; you don't need AI to speak Marathi to use those.

choices.label: Use only Marathi-trained models
choices.explanation: There aren't really good ones at this scale yet. You're picking weaker tools to avoid an easy translation step you do anyway.

questions.stem: A 14-day classroom AI experiment passes the "is this real" test only if it has at least two of:

choices.label: A baseline number captured before day 1
choices.explanation: Yes. No baseline, no comparison.

choices.label: A specific numeric outcome (e.g. 'weekly quiz average', 'minutes I spend on prep')
choices.explanation: Yes. Vague outcomes ('students seemed engaged') aren't measurable.

choices.label: A new AI tool every 2 days to test variety
choices.explanation: No. Switching the tool every 2 days means you're testing 7 things, none of them properly. Confounded variables, useless conclusion.

choices.label: A pre-committed kill criterion ("if X drops, I stop")
choices.explanation: Strictly speaking this strengthens the experiment, but it's not as load-bearing as baseline + numeric outcome. Pick the two that are; this is the third nice-to-have.

questions.stem: Which of these is the cleanest example of "brief AI like a student teacher"?

choices.label: "Make a lesson on the French Revolution."
choices.explanation: Same instruction you'd give an exhausted intern at midnight. Output quality follows input quality.

choices.label: "Make a 30-minute lesson on the French Revolution for Class 9 ICSE. Open with a hook tied to mob behaviour, end with a 5-minute discussion question. Mid-lesson, 1 short primary-source extract. Indian context welcome."
choices.explanation: Correct. Audience, time, structure, named anchors, locale. A new student teacher could deliver this.

choices.label: "Lesson on French Revolution. 9th. ICSE."
choices.explanation: Better than option A but still missing structure and outcome. You'll iterate three times to get to where option B starts.

choices.label: "French Revolution."
choices.explanation: This is a Wikipedia search, not a brief.

questions.stem: You read AI-generated feedback before sending it. You spot one phrase that doesn't sound like you ("I am thrilled by your insightful contribution"). The right move:

choices.label: Rewrite that one phrase in your own voice and send
choices.explanation: Correct. The point of reviewing AI feedback isn't to ship verbatim; it's to ship something that sounds like the teacher the child knows. Five-second fix, big trust dividend.

choices.label: Send it; the child won't notice
choices.explanation: They notice. Children are pattern matchers. "This doesn't sound like ma'am" is a thought you do not want planted.

choices.label: Throw the AI draft away and rewrite from scratch
choices.explanation: Possible, but wasteful. You used AI for the heavy lift; one phrase doesn't invalidate ten paragraphs.

choices.label: Ask the AI to rewrite without using the word 'thrilled'
choices.explanation: More iterations to dodge a 10-second manual edit. Voice is yours; do the edit.

questions.stem: Which of these are good reasons to *not* use AI in a particular lesson, even when it would save time?

choices.label: The lesson's purpose is for students to struggle with a problem unaided to build resilience
choices.explanation: Yes. If the friction is the lesson, removing the friction with AI defeats the lesson.

choices.label: You're tired and want a break
choices.explanation: That's a reason to *use* AI, not avoid it. Tired teachers ship worse lessons; AI-assisted prep at 80% is better than fully manual prep at 60%.

choices.label: The content is one you teach with strong personal voice and stories
choices.explanation: Yes. A signature class on Partition is yours; AI dilutes the voice that makes it land.

choices.label: AI made a small factual error last time
choices.explanation: Mitigated by review, not by abandonment. One wrong fact is a process problem, not a tool problem.

questions.stem: Principal Priya asks: "Should we ban AI in homework?" The single most useful clarifying question is:

choices.label: "Which subjects? Which grades? Which type of homework?"
choices.explanation: Correct. "Ban AI in homework" is a five-policy question pretending to be one. Class 4 craft project and Class 11 essay aren't the same problem.

choices.label: "What detection tool will we use?"
choices.explanation: Detection-first thinking is downstream of policy; the policy isn't defined yet.

choices.label: "What's the punishment?"
choices.explanation: Same — punishment without scope is a policy that lawyers itself. Scope first.

choices.label: "Can we just ban phones?"
choices.explanation: Different problem. Phones aren't the only access path.

questions.stem: Your Class 11 student submits a debate speech that is structurally perfect, grammatically tight, and emotionally hollow. You suspect AI. The honesty-design move that respects the student is:

choices.label: Have her deliver a 90-second extempore extension on the same topic in class tomorrow
choices.explanation: Correct. Extempore reveals whether the argument lives inside her or in a chat window. No accusation needed; performance speaks.

choices.label: Confront her in front of the class to make an example
choices.explanation: Public shame is a permanent solution to a possibly-not-permanent problem. Even if you're right, you've burned the relationship.

choices.label: Quietly mark it lower without saying why
choices.explanation: Worst of both worlds. She doesn't learn what happened; you don't learn whether you were right.

choices.label: Ask the AI detector to confirm before you decide
choices.explanation: Detectors are weak. The 90-second extempore tells you in 90 seconds what the detector won't tell you in 90 minutes.

questions.stem: You're three weeks in. The data from your 14-day AI experiment shows: prep time fell 40%, weekly test averages unchanged, but student-reported "I feel my teacher knows me" fell 1.2 points. Pick the *correct* readings.

choices.label: Time saved is real and worth keeping; the relationship score is the warning
choices.explanation: Yes. A win on the boring 80% with a loss on the human 20% is the exact pattern this course teaches you to spot. Don't kill the time saving; redirect it.

choices.label: Test averages didn't move, so the experiment failed
choices.explanation: Test averages were unchanged. That's a *neutral* finding, not failure. Failure was somewhere else, and you have to read all three numbers to see it.

choices.label: The 40% time saved should be redirected toward 1-on-1 student check-ins
choices.explanation: Yes. This is the whole game: you didn't save time to leave early; you saved time to be more present where AI cannot be.

choices.label: Roll the experiment out school-wide immediately
choices.explanation: Not yet. The relationship signal is unresolved; school-wide rollout amplifies an unsolved problem.

questions.stem: After this course, your sharpest one-line definition of "AI as teaching assistant, not replacement" is:

choices.label: AI does the boring 80%; you protect the human 20%
choices.explanation: Correct. The line is real and load-bearing. Everything else in the course is a corollary.

choices.label: AI is a junior colleague who never sleeps
choices.explanation: Pleasant metaphor; insufficient discipline. A junior colleague has judgment; AI has fluency.

choices.label: AI is just another EdTech wave
choices.explanation: Cynical undersell. EdTech mostly didn't change daily prep. Generative AI does, when used with the line drawn correctly.

choices.label: Use AI everywhere except for grading
choices.explanation: Too narrow. The boring/human line is finer than that — there's grading-shaped work AI can absolutely help with (rubric drafting, calibration), and there's non-grading work it shouldn't touch (a parent call about a sensitive child).

project.title: Capstone: Draft a 2-Page AI Policy for Your Principal
project.prompt:
**The ask.**

Principal Priya catches you outside the staff room. "In two weeks, the trustees want a school AI policy. Single page if possible, two pages max. Something we can defend to parents *and* still let our better teachers actually use AI. You teach a senior class and you've been reading about this — can you draft it?"

She walks off before you can ask the right question.

**Your job.**

Write the policy. It should answer, in plain prose:

1. **Where AI is encouraged.** Specific use cases: lesson prep, draft feedback, rubric scaffolding, exit tickets. Name them.
2. **Where AI is restricted, and why.** In-class assessments, sensitive parent communications, condolence letters, marks-of-record. Be specific about the *why*; banning by category is lazy.
3. **What students may and may not do.** A short, kind student-facing paragraph. The student is not the enemy.
4. **Detection and false-positive policy.** What you will and will not do when an AI detector flags an essay. Riya from Class 11 should not lose her board year because of a probability score.
5. **A 14-day pilot proposal.** The first thing you will measure, the kill criterion, the three numbers tracked. One paragraph.

**Constraints.**

- 2 pages max. Trustees do not read 6 pages.
- Voice should sound like a teacher who has *taught*, not a consultant. Specific examples beat policy jargon.
- At least one paragraph must explicitly identify what *cannot* be measured (the human 20%) and how the policy protects it.
- Pre-empt at least one parent objection ("my child should not have to compete with AI-assisted classmates").

**Submit.**

- The 2-page policy as a single document.
- A separate 200-word note to Principal Priya explaining the *one* clarifying question you would have asked her if she hadn't walked off.

levels.label: Every restriction is justified by a specific failure mode (false positives, AI grading meaning poorly, condolence-letter dilution); the policy survives a hostile parent and a sceptical trustee
Most restrictions are justified, but one or two read as cargo-cult bans
Restrictions are by category ("AI not allowed in homework") with no failure mode named

Treats students as collaborators, not adversaries; the human 20% is named and protected by at least one concrete clause; the false-positive policy specifically protects the strongest writers from being punished by detectors
Acknowledges the human 20% but only in abstract language; the false-positive policy is implied, not stated
Treats AI as a discipline problem; students-as-suspects framing dominates

Reads like a teacher with chalk on her hands wrote it; specific examples (CBSE Class 10 essay, JEE practice set, Marathi-medium constraint) ground the policy; the clarifying-question note shows you saw the unstated assumption Principal Priya was making
Clear writing, but generic examples that could apply to any school anywhere
Policy jargon, no specific examples, the clarifying question is also generic
